docs.title: Audit trail
docs.text:
In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

FastAPIAudit records the sensitive actions: who did what to which resource, whether it worked, and the request it came from. As a dependency, it writes the event when the endpoint ends:

from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import Depends

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPIAudit
from fastapi_alcazaba.audit import AuditEntry

audit = FastAPIAudit(signing_key=settings.audit_signing_key)
deleting = audit.action("invoice.delete", resource="invoice:{invoice_id}")


@app.delete("/invoices/{invoice_id}", status_code=204)
async def delete_invoice(
    invoice_id: int,
    entry: Annotated[AuditEntry, Depends(deleting)],  # first: it records refusals too
    user: Annotated[User, Depends(current_user)],
) -> None:
    entry.actor = user.id
    entry.details["amount"] = await invoices.delete(invoice_id, owner=user.id)
  • How it ended: success when the endpoint returns, denied when it raises a 401 or a 403 (1008 for WebSockets), failure otherwise, with the exception's type and status, never its message: messages carry data. Declared before the dependency that authenticates, the audit dependency also records the requests that one refuses, with the resource from the path. An endpoint that answers an error without raising sets entry.outcome; entry.reason says why.
  • Outside endpoints: await audit.log("user.login", outcome="failure", reason="wrong password", request=request) writes one event, and async with audit.record("backup.restore", actor="cron") one for a block of code (a job, a task), which fails when it raises or is cancelled.
  • Correlation: each event has the request ID (with RequestIDMiddleware), the OpenTelemetry trace, the method, the route template (/invoices/{invoice_id}, never the path, which may carry tokens) and the client's address as the server reports it (see client_ip behind a proxy).
  • No secrets: in details, the values under keys that name one (password, newPassword, X-Api-Key, refresh_token, session_id, cookie, card_number…: SENSITIVE_WORDS, plus yours with redact=["iban"]) and the strings that look like credentials (Bearer …, JWTs, private keys) are recorded as [redacted]. Objects and bytes are recorded by their type, not their content; strings are cut at 500 characters, lists and dicts at 50 items and 4 levels. Give actor and resource IDs, not e-mail addresses.
  • Where they go: to the logger fastapi_alcazaba.audit.events, at INFO, one line of JSON per event, ASCII only so that nothing in it splits a line: give it a handler of its own and let the log pipeline ship it to storage that can't be rewritten. If that logger outputs nothing (no handler, the root logger at WARNING), it says so once. sinks= takes others: any object with async def write(event), such as one inserting into a table, and MemoryAuditSink for tests.
  • Signed and chained: with a signing_key (32 bytes or more, the same in every process; a list to rotate it, the first signs), each event is signed with HMAC-SHA256 and carries the signature of the previous one of its stream (one per process), numbered. verify_audit_trail(events, key) lists the events altered, forged, missing or out of their chain, from AuditEvents or the JSON lines read back. The signature covers fastapi_alcazaba/audit2, a NUL byte and the event's RFC 8785 canonical JSON without its signature (fastapi_alcazaba.core.canonical_json): any language with a JCS library checks it the same way, a SIEM or an auditor's script included. For that, details keep to I-JSON: integers beyond 2⁵³ are recorded as text, lone surrogates as U+FFFD. It can't tell that the newest events were removed, and whoever has the key can rewrite the trail: keep it from the people whose actions are recorded.
  • Delivery: a sink that fails or takes longer than timeout (5 s) is logged at ERROR with the event, so that it isn't lost, and counted; the other sinks still get it, and an event is written even when its request is cancelled meanwhile. The action isn't undone or refused for it: when an action mustn't happen unrecorded, write the record in the action's own database transaction.
import json

from fastapi_alcazaba.audit import verify_audit_trail

with open("audit.log") as lines:
    events = [json.loads(line) for line in lines]
problems = verify_audit_trail(events, settings.audit_signing_key)

docs.title: API keys, tokens and codes
docs.text:
Credentials kept only as digests: API keys with scopes and expiry, revoked tokens and one-time codes.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
FastAPIAPIKeys authenticates machine clients by an API key. It generates the keys and checks them; your database keeps a record of each, never the key itself:

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth import FastAPIAPIKeys


async def load_key(key_id: str) -> ApiKeyRow | None:  # any object with digest, scopes, expires_at
    return await db.get(ApiKeyRow, key_id)


keys = FastAPIAPIKeys(load_key, pepper=settings.api_key_pepper, bearer=True)


@app.post("/api-keys")
async def create_key(user: Annotated[User, Depends(current_user)]) -> dict[str, str]:
    new = keys.generate(scopes=["orders:read"], expires_at=datetime.now(UTC) + timedelta(days=90))
    await db.add(ApiKeyRow(owner=user.id, **dataclasses.asdict(new.record)))
    return {"key": new.key}  # shown once: only its digest is stored


@app.get("/orders")
async def orders(key: Annotated[ApiKeyRow, Depends(keys.require("orders:read"))]) -> list[Order]:
    return await db.orders(owner=key.owner)
  • Key format: ak_<id>_<secret> (prefix changes ak; sk_live works too): an 80-bit id that finds the record and a 256-bit secret, in lowercase base32. A distinctive prefix lets secret scanners (GitHub's, GitLab's) spot leaked keys.
  • Stored as a digest: the record holds a SHA-256 digest of the secret, bound to the key's id. Random 256-bit secrets don't need a slow password hash. With a pepper (a server secret of at least 32 bytes, kept out of the database) the digest is an HMAC, so a copy of the database alone can't even test a guess. A list of peppers rotates them: the first one makes new keys, all of them are accepted.
  • Your database: lookup(key_id) returns your row, async or not (a plain function runs in a thread, like FastAPI's sync dependencies), and the dependency returns that same row. Any object with digest, scopes (a collection, or a space-separated string) and expires_at works; APIKeyRecord is what generate() gives.
  • Where the key comes from: the X-API-Key header (header=...) and, with bearer=True, Authorization: Bearer <key>. Both appear in the OpenAPI schema, for the docs' Authorize button.
  • One answer: a missing, malformed, unknown, wrong or expired key gets the same 401, with WWW-Authenticate; the secret is compared in constant time, and malformed keys don't reach lookup. keys.require("a", "b") adds a 403 for a valid key without all those scopes (with an RFC 6750 insufficient_scope challenge in bearer mode). Keys and secrets are never logged.
  • Revocation: delete the record, or set its expires_at in the past (naive datetimes are taken as UTC). cache_ttl keeps looked-up records in each process for that many seconds to spare the database, so a revocation then takes up to cache_ttl to reach every process; keys.forget(key_id) drops one from this process at once. Unknown ids are never cached.
  • Floods: each request with a well-formed key costs a lookup: put a FastAPIRateLimiter in front.
  • Without a dependency: await keys.authenticate(key) for keys that come some other way (a WebSocket message).

docs.title: Revoked tokens and one-time codes
docs.text:
A JWT can't be taken back once issued. TokenBlocklist keeps the revoked ones in the cache's backend, shared by every process, until they would have expired anyway:

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth import OneTimeCodes, TokenBlocklist

blocklist = TokenBlocklist()  # FastAPICache's backend; or TokenBlocklist(cache)


async def current_user(claims: Annotated[dict[str, Any], Depends(decode_jwt)]) -> str:
    sub, iat = claims["sub"], claims["iat"]
    if await blocklist.is_revoked(claims["jti"], subject=sub, issued_at=iat):
        raise HTTPException(401)
    return sub


@app.post("/logout")
async def logout(claims: Annotated[dict[str, Any], Depends(decode_jwt)]) -> None:
    await blocklist.revoke(claims["jti"], expires_at=claims["exp"])


@app.post("/password")
async def change_password(user: Annotated[str, Depends(current_user)]) -> Token:
    ...
    await blocklist.revoke_subject(user, ttl=TOKEN_LIFETIME)  # log out everywhere
    return issue_token(user)  # issued now: still valid

OneTimeCodes are the codes you send by e-mail or SMS:

codes = OneTimeCodes(secret=settings.otp_secret)  # secrets.token_urlsafe(32)


@app.post("/login/code", dependencies=[Depends(FastAPIRateLimiter(times=3, minutes=15))])
async def send_code(email: str) -> None:
    await send_email(email, await codes.issue(email, purpose="login"))


@app.post("/login")
async def login(email: str, code: str) -> Token:
    if not await codes.verify(email, code, purpose="login"):
        raise HTTPException(400, "Invalid or expired code")
    ...
  • Nothing in clear: token ids and subjects are stored as SHA-256 digests. Codes are stored as an HMAC with secret, bound to their subject and purpose: a plain digest of a 6-digit code is brute-forced in milliseconds by whoever reads the backend. A list of secrets rotates them.
  • Expiry: each revocation lasts while the token could still be accepted (exp, plus leeway, 60 s by default, for what your JWT library tolerates). Codes last ttl seconds (300).
  • Log out everywhere: revoke_subject refuses the tokens issued before the current second. iat has whole seconds, so the token you issue right after for the current session stays valid.
  • Guesses and single use: every guess counts, malformed ones included, and a code is lost after max_attempts (5). Of several requests with the right code at the same time, only one succeeds. Issuing a code replaces the previous one and gives the attempts again: rate-limit the route that issues them.
  • Every process sees them at once: they're read from the shared backend, never from TieredBackend's copies in each process. On DynamoDB, whose reads are eventually consistent, a revocation or a new code can take about a second to reach every process.
  • Failures: if the backend fails, is_revoked refuses tokens (fail_open=True accepts them), verify returns False, and revoke, revoke_subject and issue raise BackendUnavailable. With a signing_key or encryption_key, revocations are sealed and planted ones are ignored. Whoever can delete keys in the backend can still un-revoke tokens.

docs.title: Authorization with Casbin
docs.text:
Who may do what to which resource, decided by a Casbin policy (ACL, RBAC, ABAC…) per route or for every request, instead of checks spread over the routes.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Casbin policies
docs.text:
FastAPICasbin lets a request through only when a Casbin policy allows it. Who may do what lives in the policy (ACL, RBAC, RBAC with domains, ABAC…), not in checks spread over the routes. The casbin extra installs PyCasbin.

A Casbin model says what a request is and how it matches the policy; the policy, who may do what. Here a request is (user, object, action), and users get permissions through roles:

model.conf
[request_definition]
r = sub, obj, act

[policy_definition]
p = sub, obj, act

[role_definition]
g = _, _

[policy_effect]
e = some(where (p.eft == allow))

[matchers]
m = g(r.sub, p.sub) && keyMatch2(r.obj, p.obj) && r.act == p.act
policy.csv
p, reader, /articles/:id, GET
p, editor, /articles/:id, PUT
p, editor, articles, publish
g, editor, reader
g, ana, editor

import casbin

from fastapi_alcazaba.authz import FastAPICasbin

enforcer = casbin.Enforcer("model.conf", "policy.csv")
authz = FastAPICasbin(enforcer, subject=current_username)  # your dependency: who's asking

# (user, path, method): may ana PUT /articles/7?
api = APIRouter(dependencies=[Depends(authz)])


# (user, *values): your own objects and actions. Both dependencies return the user.
@app.post("/articles/{article_id}/publish")
async def publish(
    article_id: int,
    editor: Annotated[str, Depends(authz.require("articles", "publish"))],
) -> Article: ...


# {name} takes a path parameter: (user, "projects/7", "archive").
archive = authz.require("projects/{project_id}", "archive")


@app.post("/projects/{project_id}/archive", dependencies=[Depends(archive)])
async def archive_project(project_id: int) -> None: ...
  • Who: subject is a FastAPI dependency that returns who makes the request: a user name, an id, or an object for ABAC matchers (r.sub.age >= 18); None when nobody is logged in. Its own dependencies (a bearer token, a session) appear in the OpenAPI schema, for the docs' Authorize button. Without one, the user of Starlette's AuthenticationMiddleware.
  • What: Depends(authz) checks the path the app routes (without the root_path a proxy or a mount adds in front) and the method; WebSockets have the action WEBSOCKET, so a policy for GET doesn't open them. authz.require(...) checks your own values instead, {name} filled from the path parameters. In keyMatch2, :name is a parameter: name objects without colons (projects/7, not project:7), or the rule for project:7 lets project:8 through.
  • Answers: a request without a subject gets a 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer (challenge=), without asking the policy; anonymous="anonymous" has the policy check it as that subject instead, for routes open to everybody (p, anonymous, /catalog, GET). A subject that the policy refuses gets a 403. WebSockets are closed with 1008 (policy violation). A path with control characters (/users/%0A) gets a 400 without asking the policy: Starlette routes it to /users/, while the policy would read the newline. With FastAPIProblemDetails, the errors are problem details.
  • In a route: authz.enforce(user, "drafts", "read") returns a bool, for what depends on the data: the items of a list, the owner of an object.
  • Fails closed: a broken model, or a request that doesn't fit it (invalid request size), raises: a 500, never a request let through. A disabled enforcer (enforcer.enable_enforce(False)) lets everything through, as Casbin does.
  • Enforcers: any of Casbin's: Enforcer, SyncedEnforcer, FastEnforcer, AsyncEnforcer (for async adapters; await enforcer.load_policy() in the lifespan). The checks run in the event loop, like an AsyncEnforcer's changes: a request never sees half a change. Casbin tries the rules one by one, a few microseconds each (about 2.5 ms per request with 1,000 rules on a laptop): give permissions to roles rather than users, and roles to users.
  • Several processes: each one has its copy of the policy. A change made in one (await enforcer.add_role_for_user(...)) reaches the database through the adapter, and the other processes when they load the policy again: a Casbin watcher (casbin-redis-watcher…) tells them.

CasbinMiddleware checks every request instead, as (user, path, method) with the user of Starlette's AuthenticationMiddleware, anonymous when there's none. Add it before AuthenticationMiddleware, so that it runs after it; the policy must then open the public routes (/docs, /login…) to anonymous:

from starlette.middleware.authentication import AuthenticationMiddleware

from fastapi_alcazaba.authz import CasbinMiddleware

app.add_middleware(CasbinMiddleware, enforcer=enforcer)
app.add_middleware(AuthenticationMiddleware, backend=JWTBackend())

It checks the path the app routes, without the root_path, and the method, WEBSOCKET for WebSockets. Refusals get a 403 with {"detail": "Forbidden"}, like FastAPI's errors (problem details with FastAPIProblemDetails), or a 401 with WWW-Authenticate when anonymous is refused, and a 400 for paths with control characters; WebSockets are closed with 1008. OPTIONS requests are checked like the others: add CORSMiddleware after CasbinMiddleware (outside it), to answer the preflights.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
Where the cache and every other tool keep their entries and their state.

Every class and function: the API reference.

  • InMemoryBackend(max_size=10_000): per process; for development, tests and single-process apps. Up to max_size cached responses, and as many keys of state (counters, revoked tokens…) in a store of their own.
  • RedisBackend(redis): redis-py client, standalone or cluster, created without decode_responses=True. Works with any server that speaks the Redis protocol (Valkey, KeyDB, Dragonfly).
  • ValkeyBackend(valkey): the same with valkey-py (valkey.asyncio, not the sync client).
  • GlideBackend(client): Valkey GLIDE, the official Valkey client with a Rust core (await GlideClient.create(...) or GlideClusterClient).
  • TieredBackend(remote, local_ttl=5): a per-process memory level in front of any of these (see "Two-level cache").
  • MemcachedBackend(client): aiomcache. Can't tell the remaining time to live.
  • DynamoBackend(table_name, region, endpoint_url=None): aiobotocore; await backend.init() first. Enable TTL on the ttl attribute of the table. endpoint_url for DynamoDB Local or LocalStack.
Backend Clear a namespace Locks Tags Rate limiter InMemory yes (one process) yes (one process) Redis, Valkey, GLIDE yes (SCAN + UNLINK) yes yes yes, one Lua script Memcached no no no yes, adding and taking back what doesn't fit DynamoDB no yes (conditional writes) no yes, a conditional write Tiered like its shared backend like its shared backend like its shared backend in its shared backend

Valkey example with valkey-py:

import valkey.asyncio

from fastapi_alcazaba.backends.valkey import ValkeyBackend

client = valkey.asyncio.from_url("valkey://localhost:6379/0")
FastAPICache.init(ValkeyBackend(client), prefix="myapp", signing_key=settings.cache_signing_key)

docs.title: Two-level cache
docs.text:
from fastapi_alcazaba.backends.tiered import TieredBackend

FastAPICache.init(TieredBackend(ValkeyBackend(client), local_ttl=5), prefix="myapp")

TieredBackend keeps a small copy of each entry in the memory of every process, in front of the shared backend: hits served from there skip the network (131 µs → 56 µs per hit against a Valkey on the same machine; more across a real network). A local copy lives at most local_ttl seconds and never longer than the shared entry.

With Redis or Valkey through redis-py/valkey-py, writes, clears and tag invalidations are also announced on a pub/sub channel (invalidation_channel), so every process drops its copy at once: a tag invalidation names the keys it deleted, also the copies of processes that only read those entries (beyond 1000 keys, every process drops all its copies). A value read while an invalidation arrives isn't kept, since it may be the old one. Copies are only kept while the process is subscribed: if the subscription drops, or the client reconnects by itself, the local level is emptied, and bypassed until it's back. The channel is read with its own timeout, so a client socket_timeout doesn't end the subscription, and pinged after 5 quiet seconds: a connection that died silently is given up within 10. With the other backends (memcached, DynamoDB, GLIDE, a valkey-py cluster) staleness is bounded by local_ttl. If the shared backend goes down, the local copies keep being served until they expire.

docs.title: Background work
docs.text:
Work outside requests, shared by every process: jobs at given times, a task queue, a leader, and locks.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Scheduled jobs
docs.text:
FastAPIScheduler runs jobs every N seconds or by a cron expression, in every process of the app, and each tick once across them all:

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPIScheduler

scheduler = FastAPIScheduler()  # FastAPICache's backend; or FastAPIScheduler(cache)


@scheduler.every(minutes=5)
async def refresh_catalog() -> None: ...


@scheduler.cron("0 3 * * *", tz="Europe/Madrid")
def nightly_report() -> None: ...  # sync jobs run in a thread


@scheduler.every(seconds=30, exclusive=False)
async def reload_settings() -> None: ...  # in every process: what each keeps in memory


app = FastAPI(lifespan=scheduler.lifespan)  # or `async with scheduler:` in your lifespan
  • Once per tick: at each tick, the processes claim it in the backend, with an atomic counter named after the job and the tick, and only the first runs it. A lock held while the job runs keeps a run that outlasts its interval from overlapping the next tick in another process (memcached can't hold locks: there, each tick still runs once, but long runs may overlap). The ticks are the same in every process: every(minutes=5) runs at :00, :05… (UTC), so keep the servers' clocks in sync (NTP). exclusive=False runs a job in every process.
  • Cron: five fields (minute, hour, day of the month, month, day of the week, Sunday being 0 or 7) with *, lists, ranges, steps and names (*/15 9-17 * * mon-fri), or @hourly, @daily, @weekly, @monthly and @yearly, in the time zone tz (UTC by default). When the clocks change it does what cronie does: a job at a fixed time runs an hour later on the day its hour is skipped and once on the day it repeats; a job with * in its minute or hour follows real time. No dependency: the parser is Alcazaba's.
  • No drift, no bursts: the next run is the next tick after the clock, not a delay after the last run ended; ticks missed while a run took longer than its interval are skipped, not run in a row afterwards.
  • Failures: an exception is logged with its traceback, counted, and the job keeps its schedule. If the backend fails, the tick is skipped (fail_open=True runs it anyway, maybe in every process).
  • Start and stop: the jobs start with the app and never hold up its startup. At shutdown, jobs waiting for their next run stop at once and running ones get grace seconds (10) before they're cancelled; a sync job's thread runs to its end. scheduler.next_run(name) says when a job runs next. A job is named after its module and function (name= for another), the name that its ticks have in the backend.

docs.title: Task queue
docs.text:
FastAPITaskQueue hands work over from an endpoint to run in the background, in this process or in any other that shares the cache's Redis or Valkey:

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPITaskQueue

queue = FastAPITaskQueue()  # FastAPICache's backend; or FastAPITaskQueue(cache)


@queue.task(retries=5)
async def send_welcome_email(user_id: int) -> None: ...


app = FastAPI(lifespan=queue.lifespan)  # this process runs tasks too


@app.post("/users")
async def create_user(user: NewUser) -> None:
    ...
    await queue.enqueue(send_welcome_email, user.id)  # delay=60 or a timedelta to wait first
  • At least once: tasks live in a Redis stream read by a consumer group, and leave it only once they've finished. A process that dies while running one, or can't reach the backend to say it finished, means that it runs again elsewhere: write tasks so that running one twice does no harm (check first whether the e-mail went out). A worker that stops answering has its tasks taken over after visibility_timeout (60 s); running tasks are kept from that by heartbeats, however long they run. A task handed out more than max_deliveries times (5) goes to the dead letters instead: it may be what kills the workers.
  • Only registered tasks run, with JSON arguments, never pickle. enqueue checks that the arguments fit the function and serialise (TypeError otherwise), up to max_payload_size bytes (64 KiB); they arrive as JSON gives them back (tuples as lists).
  • Sealed: with a signing_key or encryption_key on the cache, every task is signed or encrypted and bound to its queue. A task that someone planted in the backend or altered is refused, logged and sent to the dead letters, never run. Without a key a warning is logged at start: whoever can write to the backend can run your tasks with arguments of their choosing.
  • Retries: a task that raises is tried again retries times (3), backoff seconds after the first failure (1), twice that after the second… up to max_backoff (600), each with jitter so that tasks that failed together (a service down) don't all retry at once. Then it goes to the dead letters with the type of its error, never the message, which may hold personal data. dead_letters() lists them, requeue_dead_letters() puts them back with their attempts reset, and discard_dead_letters(ids) deletes them.
  • Delayed tasks and retries wait in a sorted set, and move to the stream when they're due in a Lua script: two processes never both move one.
  • Bounded: the queue holds at most max_length tasks (100,000: waiting, running or delayed), and enqueue raises QueueFull beyond, instead of dropping any; about max_dead_letters (10,000) are kept. pending() counts the tasks that haven't finished.
  • Workers: start() and stop(), lifespan or async with, running concurrency tasks at a time (10) in each process; sync functions run in a thread. stop() takes no more tasks and gives the running ones grace seconds (10); those still running then are cancelled and go back to the queue at once (a sync task's thread can't be stopped: it runs to its end, so that task may run twice). A process that only runs tasks: async with queue: await asyncio.Event().wait().
  • Backends: Redis 6.2+ or Valkey through RedisBackend or ValkeyBackend (or a TieredBackend in front of one), clusters included: a queue's keys share a hash tag. Other backends raise NotImplementedError. Its keys are state keys, which clear() never deletes.
  • Small on purpose: no results, priorities or workflows. Each run is the root of a trace of its own, linked to the span of the request that enqueued it.

docs.title: Leader election
docs.text:
FastAPILeader elects one process among all those sharing the backend, for work that must run in exactly one of them all the time (a queue consumer, an outbox relay, a watcher) rather than at given times (that's the scheduler):

from fastapi_alcazaba.background import FastAPILeader

leader = FastAPILeader("outbox")  # FastAPICache's backend; or FastAPILeader("outbox", cache=cache)


@leader.run
async def relay_outbox() -> None:
    while True:
        await relay_pending()
        await asyncio.sleep(1)


app = FastAPI(lifespan=leader.lifespan)  # or `async with leader:` in your lifespan

...
if leader.is_leader:  # anywhere, sync code included
    ...
  • Election: every process campaigns for a lock named after the leader, renewed every ttl / 3 seconds (ttl is 15 by default). The one that takes it leads and runs the functions given to run; the others try again every ttl / 3 seconds or so, with jitter.
  • Hand-over: a leader that stops releases the lock, and another process takes over within ttl / 3 seconds; one that dies, within ttl and a third. A leader that loses the lock (its renewals couldn't keep up) cancels its functions within a second and campaigns again; at the next election they run again.
  • Functions: async, without arguments, added before start(). They're cancelled when the leadership ends and must let the cancellation through. An exception is logged with its traceback; the process keeps leading.
  • Failures: while the backend is down nobody is elected, and a leader that can't renew steps down when its lock expires: no leader is better than two. memcached can't hold locks.
  • Limits: a leader that stalls for longer than ttl (a long pause, a network partition) can overlap the next one for a moment. Check is_leader between the steps of long work, and keep that work idempotent.

docs.title: Locks
docs.text:
A lock shared by every process and container, for work that only one of them must do at a time:

from fastapi_alcazaba.background import LockNotAcquired


async def nightly_report() -> None:  # every instance runs it; one builds the report
    try:
        async with FastAPICache.lock("nightly-report", ttl=60):  # or cache.lock(...)
            await build_report()
    except LockNotAcquired:
        pass  # another instance is on it
  • Expiry and renewal: a lock expires after ttl seconds, so a holder that dies doesn't keep it forever; while it's held, a background task renews it every ttl / 3.
  • Only the holder releases or renews it: each acquisition has a random token, checked by a Lua script on Redis, Valkey and GLIDE and by conditional writes on DynamoDB (in memory, within one process). memcached can't hold locks. On DynamoDB, expiry compares the clocks of the app's servers: keep them in sync (NTP). A custom backend written for 0.1 has no extend_lock: use renew=False there, with a ttl longer than the work.
  • Waiting: wait=0 (the default) tries once, wait=5 keeps trying for 5 seconds, wait=None as long as it takes. acquire() and release() work without async with.
  • Failures: if the backend fails, acquire() raises BackendUnavailable: without it nobody can tell who holds the lock.
  • Limits: a holder that stalls for longer than ttl (a long pause, a network partition) loses the lock while it still runs. lock.held turns False when the renewals couldn't keep up: check it between the steps of long jobs, and make work that must never overlap idempotent too.

docs.title: Sessions, CSRF and security headers
docs.text:
What an app that browsers use needs: sessions it can revoke, requests from other sites refused, and the headers and limits every response should carry.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Server-side sessions
docs.text:
Starlette's SessionMiddleware keeps the whole session in a signed cookie: the client can read it (it's only base64), it can't be revoked (a copied cookie keeps working after logout, until it expires) and it can't hold much more than 4 KB. ServerSessionMiddleware keeps the data in the cache's backend instead, and the cookie only carries a random id; request.session works the same:

from fastapi_alcazaba.security import ServerSessionMiddleware, clear_session, rotate_session

app.add_middleware(ServerSessionMiddleware, max_age=8 * 3600, idle_timeout=1800)


@app.post("/login")
async def login(request: Request, form: Annotated[Login, Form()]) -> RedirectResponse:
    user = await authenticate(form)
    request.session["user_id"] = user.id
    rotate_session(request)  # a new id: one planted in the browser before is now worthless
    return RedirectResponse("/", status_code=303)


@app.post("/logout")
async def logout(request: Request) -> RedirectResponse:
    clear_session(request)  # deleted from the backend: a copied cookie is worth nothing now
    return RedirectResponse("/", status_code=303)
  • The cookie holds 256 random bits (secrets.token_urlsafe(32)), HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite=Lax by default, with Max-Age = max_age. Use cookie_name="__Host-session" so that a sibling subdomain can't plant one (cookie tossing).
  • The backend keeps the data under a SHA-256 digest of the id (whoever reads the keys can't use them as cookies), sealed with the cache's signing_key or encryption_key (use the latter when sessions hold personal data). Without either, whoever can write to the backend can forge a session, and a warning is logged. With a TieredBackend only the shared tier is used, so a logout is seen by every process at once.
  • Saved only when it changed, nested changes included (request.session["cart"].append(...)), when the response starts. Empty sessions aren't stored and get no cookie; a session the app empties is deleted and its cookie expired. Responses that read it get Vary: Cookie, and those that set the cookie Cache-Control: no-store unless they set their own.
  • New ids are always the server's: a cookie whose session doesn't exist (expired, made up) never becomes the id of a new session. rotate_session gives a new id with the same data (and a fresh max_age) at login, against session fixation; clear_session deletes the session and expires the cookie at logout, and data stored afterwards goes to a new session.
  • Expiry: max_age seconds after creation or rotation, and idle_timeout seconds without requests (refreshed in the backend at most every tenth of it, not on every request). Both are checked when the session is read, and the backend drops it then as well.
  • JSON only, up to max_size bytes (16 KiB): more, or a value that isn't JSON, raises when the response starts.
  • Backend failures: if the session can't be read, the request goes on with an empty one (anonymous, which fails closed) and a warning. Changing it then, or failing to save, rotate or clear it, replaces the response with a 503 and leaves the cookie alone: the response would claim a login or a logout that didn't happen. Concurrent requests of one session: the last save wins.
  • WebSockets get websocket.session too, read-only (rotate_session and clear_session raise there). A plain ASGI middleware: streaming responses still stream.

docs.title: CSRF protection
docs.text:
A page on another site can make the user's browser send a form, or a fetch, to your app, and the browser adds the user's cookies by itself. CSRFMiddleware refuses those requests with a 403, from the headers browsers send to say where a request comes from:

from fastapi_alcazaba.security import CSRFMiddleware

app.add_middleware(
    CSRFMiddleware,
    trusted_origins=["https://admin.example.com"],  # other origins whose pages may post here
    exempt_paths=["/webhooks"],  # signed in their own way
)
  • Fetch metadata first: every current browser sends Sec-Fetch-Site. same-origin (and none, a request the user typed) goes through; same-site and cross-site are refused unless their Origin is in trusted_origins. Sibling subdomains are other origins too.
  • Older browsers: without Sec-Fetch-Site, the Origin header (or else the Referer) must be the app's own origin or a trusted one. Origin: null (sandboxed frames, redirects) is refused, and so is a request with neither header.
  • Only what the browser adds by itself is protected: requests without cookies or remembered HTTP authentication (Basic, Digest, Negotiate, NTLM) go through, so APIs that take a bearer token in a header keep working from anywhere (a page on another site can't set the header). Except form submissions from other sites (Sec-Fetch-Mode other than cors): before the user has a cookie they would log the browser into the attacker's account (login CSRF). check_all=True checks every request, for apps that trust TLS client certificates or the network.
  • Safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE) always go through: they mustn't change anything.
  • The app's own origin is the scheme and the Host header as the server sees them. Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, let the server trust it (uvicorn --proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips=<proxy address>) and have the proxy pass Host on; otherwise every request looks cross-site, so list the public origin in trusted_origins.
  • Double-submit token for single-page apps, as defence in depth: with require_token=True every response to a request without a valid token sets a random one (256 bits) in the __Host-csrftoken cookie (readable by JavaScript, Secure, SameSite=Lax, the __Host- prefix keeps sibling subdomains from planting one), also in request.state.csrf_token. Requests with cookies must send it back in X-CSRF-Token; it's compared in constant time. A browser that sends neither Origin nor Referer passes with a valid token. HTML forms can't set headers, so with require_token=True every form that changes something must be sent by JavaScript (fetch with the header), the login form included; apps with plain HTML forms leave it off and rely on the origin checks, which protect them on their own.
  • WebSockets: browsers don't apply CORS to WebSocket handshakes, so any site could open one with the user's cookies and talk to it (cross-site WebSocket hijacking). Handshakes with cookies get the same checks and are closed with 1008 before they're accepted (the server answers 403); handshakes without Origin aren't from a browser and go through.
  • Refusals are logged at INFO with the method and the reason (never cookies or tokens), and counted in fastapi_alcazaba.csrf.refused. A plain ASGI middleware: streaming responses still stream.

docs.title: Security headers and body size
docs.text:
Two ASGI middlewares for what FastAPI leaves to the deployment:

from fastapi_alcazaba.security import BodySizeLimitMiddleware, SecurityHeadersMiddleware

app.add_middleware(
    BodySizeLimitMiddleware,
    max_size=1_048_576,  # 1 MiB
    paths={"/uploads": 50 * 1_048_576, "/internal/stream": None},
)
app.add_middleware(SecurityHeadersMiddleware)  # last: the outermost
  • Security headers: the OWASP REST ones: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, Referrer-Policy: no-referrer and Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin. Headers the app sets itself are never overwritten; headers= adds others or changes the defaults (None removes one). Add it last, the outermost, so that the answers of the middlewares inside it (BodySizeLimitMiddleware's 400 and 413) get them too. Starlette's 500 for an unhandled exception never does: ServerErrorMiddleware wraps every middleware you add.
  • HSTS only on HTTPS requests: browsers ignore it over plain HTTP, and on a development localhost it would stick. Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, let the server trust it (uvicorn --proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips=<proxy address>).
  • Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none' for everything that isn't HTML (nothing in a JSON response should load anything). HTML responses get html_csp, None by default, so that the Swagger UI and ReDoc, which load scripts from a CDN, keep working.
  • Body size: FastAPI has no limit of its own; a client could send an endless body that the app reads into memory. A Content-Length over the limit gets a 413 before the app runs, a malformed or ambiguous one a 400. Bodies without one (chunked) are counted while the app reads them and refused once they pass the limit, also when FastAPI parses them into a model. paths sets other limits by path prefix (the longest wins, None for no limit), matched like the routes, without the root_path.
  • Both are plain ASGI middlewares, not BaseHTTPMiddleware: streaming responses still stream, and WebSockets go through untouched.

docs.title: Response cache
docs.text:
@cache for endpoints and functions, and Cache behind it: what each entry is stored under, for how long, and how it's kept safe. The quick start sets one up.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: FastAPICache.init()
docs.text:
Call it once, at startup (in the lifespan).

Parameter Default Description backend InMemoryBackend, RedisBackend, ValkeyBackend, GlideBackend, MemcachedBackend or DynamoBackend prefix "" prefix of every key expire None default time to live, in seconds coder JsonCoder how values are stored key_builder default_key_builder builds keys from the function and its arguments cache_status "Alcazaba" this cache's name in the Cache-Status header (RFC 9211); None to leave it out enable True False turns the cache off signing_key None secret of 32+ bytes to sign entries; a list rotates keys (the first signs) encryption_key None secret of 32+ bytes to sign and encrypt entries (crypto extra); instead of signing_key compression None "zstd" or "zlib": store large entries compressed compression_min_size 1024 bytes; smaller entries aren't compressed compression_level codec's default vary_headers ("authorization", "cookie") request headers that give each value its own entry respect_cache_control False let clients skip the cache with no-cache/no-store single_flight True concurrent misses for one key compute once, per process backend_timeout 1.0 seconds a backend call may take before the request goes on without cache circuit_breaker_failures 5 consecutive failures that stop the backend calls; None disables the breaker circuit_breaker_reset 30.0 seconds before trying the backend again max_value_size None bytes; larger values aren't stored distributed_lock False one process computes a missing value while the others wait for it lock_timeout 10.0 seconds before a lock expires (if its holder dies) lock_wait 5.0 seconds a process waits for another one's value before computing it early_refresh None fraction of the lifetime, at its end, in which hits may refresh the entry metrics True OpenTelemetry metrics, with the otel extra meter_provider global OpenTelemetry meter provider tracing True OpenTelemetry spans, with the otel extra tracer_provider global OpenTelemetry tracer provider

docs.title: @cache()
docs.text:
Parameter Default Description expire from init time to live, in seconds coder from init key_builder from init namespace "" group of entries, for FastAPICache.clear(namespace=...) injected_dependency_namespace "__fastapi_alcazaba" prefix of the Request/Response parameters added to the endpoint exclude_params None arguments left out of the key (a nonce, a database session…) vary_headers from init () for responses that are the same for everybody respect_cache_control from init stale_while_revalidate None adds that Cache-Control directive single_flight from init max_value_size from init distributed_lock from init early_refresh from init tags None names to invalidate the entry by: a list, or a function of the arguments

Delete entries with await FastAPICache.clear(namespace="products"), one entry with await FastAPICache.clear(key=...), or by tag with await FastAPICache.invalidate_tags(...). clear() without arguments deletes every cached response under the prefix. Locks, rate-limit counters, revoked tokens, one-time codes and idempotency records are kept apart, under {prefix}! instead of {prefix}:, so no clear() frees a held lock, resets a limit or takes a revocation back; InMemoryBackend keeps them apart too, so caching many responses never evicts them.

docs.title: Several caches, dependency injection and get_or_set
docs.text:
FastAPICache is one global cache. For one cache per app, or several with different settings, create Cache instances (same arguments as FastAPICache.init()) and decorate with their cached():

from fastapi_alcazaba import Cache, get_cache

public_cache = Cache(RedisBackend(redis), prefix="public", vary_headers=())
private_cache = Cache(
    RedisBackend(redis), prefix="private", encryption_key=settings.cache_encryption_key
)
private_cache.install(app)  # what get_cache returns


@app.get("/catalog")
@public_cache.cached(expire=600)
async def catalog() -> list[Product]: ...


@app.get("/me/orders")
async def orders(
    user: Annotated[User, Depends(current_user)], cache: Annotated[Cache, Depends(get_cache)]
) -> list[Order]:
    # Anything worth caching that doesn't fit a decorator; the key is hashed before storing.
    return await cache.get_or_set(f"orders:{user.id}", lambda: load_orders(user.id), expire=60)

get_or_set goes through the same pipeline as the decorator (signing or encryption, compression, single flight, locks, tags). Close the backend at shutdown with await cache.close().

docs.title: Invalidating by tag
docs.text:
Tag entries when they're cached and delete them all when the data changes, without knowing their keys:

@app.get("/products/{product_id}")
@cache(expire=600, tags=lambda product_id, **_: [f"product:{product_id}", "catalog"])
async def product(product_id: int) -> Product: ...


@app.put("/products/{product_id}")
async def update_product(product_id: int, data: Product) -> Product:
    saved = save(product_id, data)
    await FastAPICache.invalidate_tags(f"product:{product_id}")
    return saved

The function receives the same arguments as the endpoint. Tags work with the in-memory, Redis, Valkey and GLIDE backends; in Redis-like servers each tag is a set that lives as long as its longest-lived entry.

docs.title: Responses in several languages
docs.text: If an endpoint translates its response according to a request header, such as Accept-Language, add that header to vary_headers (@cache(vary_headers=["accept-language"])), or a user would get the cached response in another user's language.

docs.title: Encrypted entries
docs.text:
FastAPICache.init(
    RedisBackend(redis),
    prefix="myapp",
    encryption_key=settings.cache_encryption_key,  # secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
)

Each entry is encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key derived (HKDF-SHA256) from the secret and a random salt, with the cache key as associated data: an entry only decrypts under its own key, and any change to it is detected. A list of secrets rotates them: the first encrypts, all of them decrypt. Encryption also authenticates the entries, so it replaces signing_key rather than adding to it. It costs a few microseconds per entry.

docs.title: Compression
docs.text:
FastAPICache.init(RedisBackend(redis), compression="zstd")  # or "zlib", no dependencies

Entries of at least compression_min_size bytes (1 KiB) are compressed when that makes them smaller; JSON lists shrink about 10-15 times with zstd, which means less memory in Redis/Valkey and less network. zstd is in the standard library from Python 3.14 (zstd extra before). Compressed entries are recognised when they're read whatever the setting, so it can be turned on or off at any time; decompression is bounded by max_value_size (64 MiB if unset), so a compressed bomb planted in the backend is rejected.

Compression happens before signing or encryption. With encryption, the size of an entry still says how compressible it was: if an attacker can both read the backend and put chosen text into a response next to a secret, that can leak information about the secret (the CRIME/BREACH family). Leave compression off for such responses.

docs.title: Coders
docs.text:
JsonCoder (the default) stores anything FastAPI can turn into JSON, through pydantic-core (Rust) when it can: about 8 times faster than jsonable_encoder() for a list of models. Annotate the return type and cache hits come back as that type (Pydantic models, dataclasses, lists of models…), validated straight from the stored bytes:

@app.get("/products")
@cache(expire=60)
async def products() -> list[Product]: ...

PickleCoder stores any picklable object. Unpickling runs code chosen by whoever wrote the bytes: use it only with a signing_key or an encryption_key (Alcazaba warns otherwise).

A custom coder subclasses fastapi_alcazaba.Coder:

import orjson
from fastapi.encoders import jsonable_encoder

from fastapi_alcazaba import Coder


class ORJsonCoder(Coder):
    @classmethod
    def encode(cls, value: Any) -> bytes:
        return orjson.dumps(value, default=jsonable_encoder)

    @classmethod
    def decode(cls, value: bytes) -> Any:
        return orjson.loads(value)

docs.title: Key builders
docs.text:
The default key is the SHA-256 of the function's module and qualified name and the repr() of its arguments, under <prefix>:<namespace>:. Arguments whose repr() changes on every call (a database session or a service injected with Depends, whose repr() shows a memory address) make every call a miss: Alcazaba warns about them (UnstableCacheKeyWarning) on the first call. Leave them out with exclude_params:

@app.get("/products")
@cache(expire=30, exclude_params=["session"])
def products(session: Annotated[Session, Depends(get_session)], page: int = 1) -> list[Product]: ...

A custom key builder receives the function, the namespace and the request:

from typing import Any

from starlette.requests import Request
from starlette.responses import Response


def request_key_builder(
    func: Any,
    namespace: str = "",
    *,
    request: Request | None = None,
    response: Response | None = None,
    args: tuple[Any, ...],
    kwargs: dict[str, Any],
) -> str:
    assert request is not None
    return ":".join(
        [
            namespace,
            request.method.lower(),
            request.url.path,
            repr(sorted(request.query_params.items())),
        ]
    )


@app.get("/")
@cache(expire=60, key_builder=request_key_builder)
async def index() -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"hello": "world"}

Whatever the key builder, Alcazaba appends a digest of the vary_headers.

docs.title: Idempotency keys
docs.text:
In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

A client that retries a POST after a timeout or a dropped connection gets the first response again, instead of creating a second order or paying twice (draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header):

from fastapi_alcazaba.idempotency import IdempotencyMiddleware, require_idempotency_key

app.add_middleware(IdempotencyMiddleware)  # the app's cache (Cache.install) or FastAPICache's


@app.post("/payments", status_code=201, dependencies=[Depends(require_idempotency_key)])
async def pay(payment: Payment) -> Receipt: ...

The client sends a fresh key with each new request, and the same one when it retries it: Idempotency-Key: "8e03978e-40d5-43e8-bc93-6894a57f9324".

  • Retries get the first response (status, headers and body) with Idempotent-Replayed: true; the endpoint runs once.
  • One at a time: a retry that arrives while the first request still runs gets a 409 with Retry-After: 1. A lock in the backend, renewed while the request runs, sees to it across processes.
  • The same key for another request (method, path, query or body) gets a 422. The body is compared byte for byte: a retry sends the same bytes, not the same JSON written another way (keys in another order, other spacing).
  • Per client: keys are looked up among the requests with the same Authorization header (hashed), so one user never gets another's response. With cookie sessions, and with access tokens that get refreshed (a retry sent with a fresh token would run again), pass identifier= returning the user's id. Requests without credentials share one space of keys, safe as long as clients make their keys random (UUIDs).
  • What's kept, and for how long: responses below 500 for expire seconds (24 hours), except those worth retrying (408, 409, 425, 429) and those about the request itself, given before the endpoint did anything (401, 403, 404, 405, 413, 415, 422 and the like): a retry gets them afresh, and nobody can fill the backend with them (FastAPI's 422 echoes the request body). Request bodies are read whole to fingerprint them, up to max_body_size (a 413 beyond); a client that goes away before sending all of it doesn't reach the endpoint. Responses above max_response_size aren't kept, so a retry runs again. The stored responses go through the cache's signing or encryption: use an encryption_key when they carry personal data.
  • Failures: if the backend fails the request gets a 503: running a payment twice is worse than refusing it. fail_open=True runs it without idempotency instead. Errors of the endpoint itself, BackendUnavailable included, are left to the app.
  • Requests without the header go through untouched. It applies to POST and PATCH (methods=), and needs a backend with locks.

docs.title: Rate and concurrency limits
docs.text:
How many requests a client may make in a window, and how many may run at the same time, across every process.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Rate limiting
docs.text:
FastAPIRateLimiter is a FastAPI dependency that lets each client make times requests per window to a route; the next ones get a 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After. Its counters live in the cache's backend, so every process and container shares them:

from functools import partial

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends
from starlette.requests import HTTPConnection

from fastapi_alcazaba.rate_limit import FastAPIRateLimiter


@app.get("/search", dependencies=[Depends(FastAPIRateLimiter(times=10, minutes=1))])
async def search(q: str) -> list[Product]: ...


def user_id(connection: HTTPConnection) -> str:  # a Request, or a WebSocket
    return connection.state.user_id  # set by your authentication middleware


# 1000 requests per hour and user, for all the routes of the router together.
api = APIRouter(
    dependencies=[Depends(FastAPIRateLimiter(1000, hours=1, name="api", identifier=user_id))]
)

# One budget across routes, of which each export takes 50.
partner_budget = partial(FastAPIRateLimiter, 1000, hours=1, name="partners", identifier=user_id)
partners = APIRouter()
partners.get("/orders", dependencies=[Depends(partner_budget())])(list_orders)
partners.get("/export", dependencies=[Depends(partner_budget(cost=50))])(export_orders)
  • Who: by default, the client's address as the ASGI server reports it (client_ip), IPv6 addresses by their /64 network: each customer gets at least a whole /64, and one budget per address would give a client 2⁶⁴ of them. Many ISPs delegate a /56 or a /48, and tunnel brokers hand out /48s for free: client_network(24, 48) groups wider networks. Behind a proxy, let the server take the address from the proxy's headers: uvicorn reads them, but only from the addresses in --forwarded-allow-ips (127.0.0.1 by default), so give it your proxy's. The limiter never reads X-Forwarded-For itself, which any client can set. identifier= counts per user, API key… Identities are hashed before they reach the backend.
  • Where: each route has its own budget, whatever its path parameters: /items/1 and /items/2 share one. Limiters with the same name and rate share one budget across routes, and cost= makes a route take more of it.
  • How: a sliding window. The count of the previous window is added in proportion to how much of it is still less than a window ago, so nobody doubles the limit around the boundary between two windows. Requests over the limit don't count: checking and counting is one atomic operation (a Lua script on Redis, Valkey and GLIDE, a conditional write on DynamoDB). A client with nothing left is then refused by each process without asking the backend, until something fits again: a flood doesn't reach the backend. limiter.forget() drops that memory (between tests; a new cache drops it too). Windows follow the clocks of the app's servers: keep them in sync (NTP).
  • What clients see: responses carry the RateLimit and RateLimit-Policy headers of the IETF draft: RateLimit: "api";r=998;t=3540 means 998 requests left, at least for the next 3540 seconds. Clients can slow down before they get a 429. headers=False leaves them out. An endpoint that returns a Response object itself gets none: FastAPI only adds the headers that dependencies set to the responses it builds from a return value. Nor do the errors it builds from an exception (a 422, an HTTPException raised after the limiter), unless FastAPIProblemDetails is installed: it adds them back. An invalid request counts too: FastAPI runs the dependencies before it answers 422.
  • Which backend: the cache= given, else the app's (Cache.install) or FastAPICache's. Every backend can keep counters; TieredBackend keeps them only in its shared backend, and FastAPICache.clear() never resets them. They go through the cache's timeout and circuit breaker: if the backend fails, requests go through (fail_open=False answers 503 instead).
  • What happens over the limit: callback(request, seconds_to_wait), by default too_many_requests (the 429). If the callback returns, the request goes on.

On a WebSocket route, the dependency limits connections (closing with 1008). Call await limiter.hit(connection, key=..., cost=...) yourself to limit anything else: it counts and returns None within the limit, else the seconds to wait. For example, the messages of a WebSocket, or the login attempts to an account:

from fastapi_alcazaba.rate_limit import FastAPIRateLimiter, too_many_requests

login_attempts = FastAPIRateLimiter(times=5, minutes=15, identifier=lambda _: "")


@app.post("/login")
async def login(request: Request, form: Annotated[LoginForm, Form()]) -> Token:
    # Five attempts per account every 15 minutes, wherever they come from.
    if (wait := await login_attempts.hit(request, key=form.username)) is not None:
        too_many_requests(request, wait)
    ...

docs.title: Concurrency limits
docs.text:
FastAPIConcurrencyLimiter limits how many requests run at the same time, across every process and container, for endpoints whose cost is how long they run (AI, OCR, PDF rendering). The rate limiter counts requests per window; this counts the ones in flight:

from fastapi_alcazaba.rate_limit import FastAPIConcurrencyLimiter
from fastapi_alcazaba.rate_limit import client_ip

ocr = FastAPIConcurrencyLimiter(4, name="ocr", wait=2)  # FastAPICache's backend, or cache=...


@app.post("/invoices/scan", dependencies=[Depends(ocr)])
async def scan(file: UploadFile) -> Invoice: ...


@app.post("/summaries", dependencies=[Depends(FastAPIConcurrencyLimiter(1, identifier=client_ip))])
async def summarise(text: str) -> Summary: ...  # one at a time per client


async def scan_pending() -> None:  # outside requests: a job, a queue consumer
    async with ocr.slot():
        ...
  • Slots in the backend: limit locks (up to 100), tried in random order so that the processes don't all queue on the first; a request holds one while it runs, renewed every ttl / 3 seconds, and the slots of a process that dies expire after ttl (60). Keys are SHA-256 digests: client identities never reach the backend in clear.
  • When it's full: a request waits up to wait seconds (0: tries once), polling with jittered backoff, then gets a 503 with Retry-After (retry_after, 1 s by default); a 429 when the limit is per client (identifier). There's no queue and no order among the waiters. WebSockets are closed with 1013 (1008 per client) and hold their slot while connected.
  • Sharing: by default each route (methods and path template) has its own slots; limiters with the same name and limit share them. slot(key=...) gives each key its own slots outside requests (it needs a name), and slot(connection=request) takes one around just the expensive part of an endpoint.
  • Streaming: the slot is released when FastAPI runs the dependency's exit code. Since FastAPI 0.118 that's after the response is sent, so a StreamingResponse keeps its slot until its last byte; Depends(limiter, scope="function") (FastAPI 0.121) releases it when the endpoint returns, before the body. FastAPI 0.115 to 0.117 release it before the response is sent: take a slot() inside the stream there.
  • Failures: if the backend fails, each process counts the slots on its own (fail_open=True, the default: at most limit per process run); fail_open=False refuses with a 503 instead (slot() raises BackendUnavailable). memcached can't hold locks.
  • Limits: like any lock on a cache-like store, a holder that stalls for longer than ttl loses its slot while it still runs, and someone else may take it. Taking a slot when most are busy costs a round trip per busy slot tried.

docs.title: Errors and observability
docs.text:
Errors that say what went wrong without leaking internals, and what tells you how the app is doing: request IDs, deadlines, health checks, metrics and traces.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Problem details
docs.text:
FastAPIProblemDetails answers errors with RFC 9457 problem details (application/problem+json) instead of FastAPI's {"detail": ...}, and without telling clients what they shouldn't know:

from fastapi_alcazaba.observability import FastAPIProblemDetails, Problem

problems = FastAPIProblemDetails()
problems.install(app)


@app.post("/orders")
async def order(item: Item) -> Order:
    if stock[item.id] < item.quantity:
        raise Problem(
            409,
            f"Only {stock[item.id]} left",
            type="https://example.com/problems/out-of-stock",
            title="Out of stock",
            extensions={"available": stock[item.id]},
        )
    ...

{"type": "https://example.com/problems/out-of-stock", "title": "Out of stock", "status": 409,
 "detail": "Only 3 left", "instance": "/orders", "available": 3, "request_id": "4bf92f35…"}
  • Members: type (about:blank unless a Problem says otherwise), title (the RFC 9110 status phrase), status, detail when there's something to tell, instance (the request's path, percent-encoded) and request_id when RequestIDMiddleware gave the request one.
  • HTTPExceptions: FastAPI's, Starlette's and their subclasses (BreakerOpen, the rate limiter's 429…) keep their headers: Retry-After, WWW-Authenticate, Allow. A 4xx's detail is sent, since it's written for clients (expose_detail=False keeps it); a 5xx's never is: an HTTPException(500, str(error)) becomes a bare 500, and the hidden detail is logged as a warning. A detail that isn't a string goes in an errors member. Codes under 400 (a redirect raised as an exception) keep FastAPI's answer.
  • Validation errors: a 422 whose errors list each error's loc, msg and type, never its input (FastAPI echoes what was sent, passwords included) nor its ctx. At most max_errors=100, so that a huge invalid body doesn't get a huge answer.
  • Unhandled exceptions: a 500 that says nothing about them. Starlette raises the exception again after the response, so the server logs it with its traceback (uvicorn's "Exception in ASGI application", with the request ID when you use RequestIDLogFilter) and TestClient raises it in tests; it isn't logged a second time. With debug=True Starlette shows its traceback page instead.
  • Problem: an HTTPException with a type URI, a title and extension members, whose names are checked (three or more letters, digits or _, starting with a letter; never a standard member) and whose values are encoded when it's raised. Its detail is always sent, also with a 5xx: you wrote it for the client. problems.response(request, Problem(...)) answers one from your own exception handlers.
  • Alcazaba's middlewares too: what they answer themselves (the 504 of a timeout, the 413 of a body too large, the 503 of maintenance, the 403 of CSRF, the idempotency errors) is a problem as well, headers such as Retry-After kept, once it's installed on the app.
  • Handlers you register for a status code or an exception subclass still win; install it before the app starts.

docs.title: Request IDs
docs.text:
RequestIDMiddleware gives every request an ID, to find all the log lines of one request and to let a client quote it when it reports an error:

import logging

from fastapi_alcazaba.observability import RequestIDLogFilter, RequestIDMiddleware, request_id

app.add_middleware(RequestIDMiddleware)  # last: the outermost

handler = logging.StreamHandler()
handler.addFilter(RequestIDLogFilter())
handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(asctime)s [%(request_id)s] %(name)s: %(message)s"))
logging.getLogger().addHandler(handler)


@app.post("/jobs")
async def create_job() -> dict[str, str | None]:
    return {"ticket": request_id()}

With uvicorn, add the filter to its handlers too ("filters": {"request_id": {"()": "fastapi_alcazaba.observability.RequestIDLogFilter"}} in its log_config), and its access and error lines carry the ID.

  • Incoming IDs: the request's X-Request-ID (header= for another) is reused when a proxy or the client set one that's safe to log: a single value matching [A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,128}. Anything else (line breaks that would forge log lines, an endless value, several values) gets a new random one, 128 bits in hex. trust_incoming=False always makes a new one.
  • Everywhere in the request: request_id() returns it in endpoints, dependencies, sync endpoints' threads and WebSockets; None outside a request. The response carries it in the same header (unless the app set that header itself), and so do WebSocket handshakes.
  • In errors: after an unhandled exception the ID stays set for the rest of the request's task, so Starlette's 500 handler and the server's error log, which run outside every middleware, still know which request failed. FastAPIProblemDetails puts it in every problem, 500s included, and in their header.
  • In logs: RequestIDLogFilter sets record.request_id (default="-" outside a request; a request_id passed in extra= is kept). Add it to handlers: a logger's filters don't see the records of its child loggers.
  • Add it last, the outermost, so that the answers of the other middlewares (a 413, a 504) carry the ID too.

docs.title: Request timeouts
docs.text:
RequestTimeoutMiddleware gives every request a deadline, so that a hung dependency or a client that trickles its body doesn't hold a request (and its database connection, its memory…) forever:

from fastapi_alcazaba.observability import RequestTimeoutMiddleware

app.add_middleware(
    RequestTimeoutMiddleware,
    timeout=30,
    paths={"/reports": 120, "/events": None},  # Server-Sent Events: no deadline
)
  • Before the response starts: at the deadline the app is cancelled, its finally blocks and the exit of its yield dependencies run, and the client gets a 504 ({"detail": "Request timed out"}, or a problem with FastAPIProblemDetails). Reading the request body counts: a client that sends it a byte at a time runs out of time too.
  • While a response streams: it's too late for a 504. The app is cancelled all the same and the TimeoutError raised again, so the server closes the connection: the client sees an incomplete body (an unfinished chunked read), never a short one that looks complete. Give streaming endpoints their own deadline in paths, or None.
  • After the response: once its last byte is sent the deadline is off, so background tasks run as long as they need.
  • Sync endpoints run in a thread that can't be interrupted: the client gets its 504 on time, but the thread runs to its end, after the exit of its yield dependencies has run. Endpoints that may hit the deadline are better async.
  • Paths: paths sets other deadlines by path prefix (the longest wins, None for none), matched like the routes, without the root_path; timeout=None leaves the other paths without one. The app's own TimeoutErrors go through untouched, and WebSockets and lifespan events too.
  • Both cases are logged as warnings with the method and the route template. A plain ASGI middleware: streaming responses still stream.

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
health_router() adds the two endpoints that load balancers and orchestrators probe:

from fastapi_alcazaba.observability import HealthCheck, health_router


async def database() -> None:
    async with engine.connect() as connection:
        await connection.execute(text("SELECT 1"))


app.include_router(
    health_router({"database": database, "search": HealthCheck(ping_search, critical=False)})
)

Point the liveness probe at /health/live and the readiness probe (or the load balancer's health check, e.g. the target group of an ECS service) at /health/ready.

  • Live vs ready: /health/live only says that the process answers. /health/ready runs the checks concurrently, each with a timeout (timeout=2.0, or the check's own), and answers 200 (ok, or degraded when only non-critical checks fail) or 503 (fail) with each check's status and duration. Keep dependencies out of liveness: a probe that checks the database gets healthy containers restarted every time it blips. A check passes when it returns anything but False without raising. Sync checks run in a daemon thread of their own, off the event loop, so one that hangs holds up neither the shutdown nor the threads of the loop's default executor; it isn't started again, under the same name in the same router, until its thread finishes.
  • The cache is checked, but isn't critical: the cache's backend (cache=, else the app's or FastAPICache's) is asked for a key under its prefix, straight, not through the circuit breaker. The cache fails open, so its outage makes the app degraded, not unready: taking every instance out of the load balancer would turn a Redis outage into a full one. include_cache=False leaves it out.
  • No leaked errors: failures are logged with their traceback and never returned: a public probe mustn't tell the world the database's hostname or connection string.
  • Probes don't pile up: concurrent /ready requests share one run of the checks, and its result answers the next ones for reuse_for=1.0 seconds, so a flood of probes doesn't flood the database. A probe that goes away doesn't cancel the run the others are waiting for.
  • The endpoints are left out of the OpenAPI schema unless include_in_schema=True; responses carry Cache-Control: no-store.

docs.title: Metrics and traces
docs.text:
Alcazaba logs under fastapi_alcazaba.* with a NullHandler, as libraries do: its warnings (a breaker that opens, maintenance turned on, a backend that fails) show once the app configures logging, e.g. logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO). uvicorn alone only configures its own loggers.

Alcazaba only uses the OpenTelemetry API (the otel extra): it records nothing until the app configures an SDK, and never configures one itself. The simplest way is OpenTelemetry's own zero-code instrumentation, with the standard variables:

pip install opentelemetry-distro opentelemetry-exporter-otlp
opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install  # instrumentations for FastAPI, httpx2, redis, SQLAlchemy…

OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=shop-api \
OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES=deployment.environment.name=production \
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=https://collector.internal:4317 \
OTEL_PYTHON_LOG_CORRELATION=true \
OTEL_PYTHON_FASTAPI_EXCLUDED_URLS="health/live,health/ready" \
opentelemetry-instrument uvicorn app:app

Give the collector's endpoint explicitly, over TLS: traces and logs carry what your app does. Then Alcazaba adds to them:

  • Spans: one per cached call (fastapi_alcazaba <function>, with fastapi_alcazaba.result: hit, miss, refresh or bypass) and, inside it, one per backend call (fastapi_alcazaba.backend get, set, lock…, with failures recorded); instrumented Redis/Valkey clients nest their own inside. Each run of a scheduled job is the root of a trace of its own (fastapi_alcazaba.scheduler <job>, failures recorded), so what the job does (queries, calls) is grouped under it instead of scattered. So is each run of a task (fastapi_alcazaba.task <task>, with its queue, ID and attempt), linked to the span that enqueued it.
  • On the request's span: the events fastapi_alcazaba.rate_limit (a request limited or unchecked), fastapi_alcazaba.breaker.refused, .opened and .closed, fastapi_alcazaba.outbound.refused (an outbound call to an origin whose breaker is open) and fastapi_alcazaba.csrf.refused, and the attribute fastapi_alcazaba.idempotency with the outcome of an Idempotency-Key.
  • Never: keys, tokens, identities, codes or request bodies. Attributes are names, routes and outcomes, few enough to keep the cardinality of the metrics low.
