docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
Switches every process sees at once: circuit breakers, maintenance mode and feature flags.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Circuit breakers
docs.text:
FastAPIBreaker stops calling a dependency that keeps failing (a database, an SDK, a service reached without httpx), so that requests fail at once instead of waiting for it, and it gets room to recover:

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPIBreaker

payments = FastAPIBreaker("payments", failure_threshold=5, reset_timeout=30, timeout=10)


@payments
async def charge(order: Order) -> Receipt:
    return await payments_sdk.charge(order.id, order.total)


async def refund(order: Order) -> None:
    async with payments.attempt():  # or around a block
        await payments_sdk.refund(order.id)
  • States: after failure_threshold consecutive failures it opens, and for reset_timeout seconds calls fail with BreakerOpen without reaching the dependency. Then a single trial call goes through: its success closes the breaker, its failure opens it again.
  • In FastAPI: BreakerOpen is an HTTPException: an endpoint that hits an open breaker answers 503 with Retry-After (the seconds until the trial), without naming the dependency.
  • What counts: exceptions in failures (any Exception by default) are failures; those in exclude mean the dependency answered (a "not found" from its SDK) and are successes; others, and a cancelled call, give no verdict. timeout bounds async calls: a slower call is cancelled, raises TimeoutError and counts as a failure. Sync code can't be interrupted, so a breaker with a timeout refuses to guard it.
  • Per process: each process keeps its own state, with no round trip on every call. Sync functions work too, also from the threads of FastAPI's pool.
  • Closed by hand: payments.reset() closes it at once and forgets the failures, when you know the dependency is back (from an admin endpoint) or between tests; failure_threshold and reset_timeout can be read back.
  • Observability: opening is logged as a warning and closing again as info, and both are counted with the calls (fastapi_alcazaba.breaker.* metrics). breaker.state says "closed", "open" or "half-open", handy in a health check: HealthCheck(lambda: payments.state != "open", critical=False).

docs.title: Maintenance mode
docs.text:
FastAPIMaintenance is a switch shared by every process; while it's on, MaintenanceMiddleware answers 503 with Retry-After to every request but the allowed ones:

from fastapi_alcazaba.rate_limit import client_ip
from fastapi_alcazaba.operations import FastAPIMaintenance, MaintenanceMiddleware

maintenance = FastAPIMaintenance()  # FastAPICache's backend; or FastAPIMaintenance(cache)
app.add_middleware(
    MaintenanceMiddleware,
    maintenance=maintenance,
    allow_paths=("/health", "/admin"),  # always served
    allow=lambda request: client_ip(request) in OFFICE,  # the team keeps working
)

await maintenance.enable("Back at 10:30", retry_after=900)  # from an admin route, a script...
await (
    maintenance.status()
)  # MaintenanceStatus(enabled=True, message=..., retry_after=900, since=...)
await maintenance.disable()
  • Shared, but not asked on every request: the state lives in the backend, and each process keeps a copy refreshed at most every refresh seconds (1 by default), so a change reaches every process within about that. status() reads the backend now; forget() drops the copy, and a new cache drops it by itself (each test's lifespan sets one up).
  • Responses: a 503 whose detail is the message ("Service Unavailable" without one), with Retry-After when given and Cache-Control: no-store. WebSockets are closed with 1013 (try again later). Lifespan events go through. A pure ASGI middleware: streaming isn't affected.
  • Exceptions: allow_paths are prefixes (/health covers /health/live, not /healthz), matched without the root_path of a proxy or a mount, and are served without reading the state. allow (sync or async) receives the request: use the address the server reports (client_ip), never X-Forwarded-For.
  • Failures: when the backend fails, each process keeps the last state it read (maintenance often means work on the backend itself: its failure mustn't reopen an app closed on purpose) and serves normally if it never read one. enable() and disable() raise BackendUnavailable: nothing changes then.
  • Integrity: with a signing_key or encryption_key on the cache the state is sealed, and a state planted in the backend by someone else is ignored; the message is capped at 1000 characters.

docs.title: Feature flags
docs.text:
FastAPIFeatureFlags keeps flags in the backend: turn features on and off for everybody, for some users or tenants, or for a percentage of them, from any process and without a deploy:

from fastapi_alcazaba.operations import FastAPIFeatureFlags

flags = FastAPIFeatureFlags()  # FastAPICache's backend; or FastAPIFeatureFlags(cache, refresh=5)

await flags.set("new-checkout", enabled=True, percentage=10, allow=["user-42"], deny=["user-7"])

if await flags.enabled("new-checkout", subject=str(user.id)):
    ...


def user_id(request: Request) -> str | None:
    return request.headers.get("x-user-id")


@app.get("/beta/report", dependencies=[Depends(flags.require("beta-report", subject=user_id))])
async def beta_report() -> Report: ...  # 404 while the flag is off for the user
  • Rules: a flag is on for a subject when it's enabled, the subject isn't in deny, and it's in allow or falls within percentage. No percentage means everybody, but only allow when there's an allow list: a flag for a few never goes to everyone by mistake. enabled=False turns it off for everyone, allow included. Without a subject, a partial rollout counts as off. An undefined flag gives default (False).
  • Sticky rollouts: a subject's place comes from a hash of the flag's name and the subject, so it keeps its answer while the percentage stays, raising the percentage only adds subjects, and each flag picks different subjects.
  • Hidden when off: require() answers FastAPI's own 404 Not Found, so the flag isn't revealed, and closes WebSockets with 1008. For subjects that need other dependencies (the current user), call enabled() from your own dependency.
  • Local copies: each process keeps the definitions it reads for refresh seconds (5), so a change reaches every process within that, and a flag costs at most one round trip per refresh. When the backend fails, the last definition read is used, or the default. get(name) reads the backend now; delete(name) removes a flag; forget() drops the copies, and a new cache drops them by itself.
  • Privacy and integrity: subjects are stored as SHA-256 digests salted with the flag's name, never in clear (at most 10,000 per list). Whoever reads the backend can still confirm a guess of a guessable subject (an e-mail address): prefer opaque ids, or give the cache an encryption_key, which encrypts the definitions. With a signing_key or encryption_key, definitions planted by someone else are ignored. Names are up to 100 letters, digits, ., _ and -.

docs.title: Production setup
docs.text: The quick start keeps everything in the process: each process has its own cache, counters and revoked tokens. In production, several processes or containers serve the app, and they share that state through a backend: Redis, Valkey, memcached or DynamoDB.

docs.title: Install the extras
docs.text:
Each backend and integration needs a library of its own, which an extra installs:

pip install fastapi-alcazaba            # in-memory backend only
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[redis]"   # or [valkey], [glide], [memcache], [dynamodb], [all]
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[otel]"    # OpenTelemetry metrics
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[crypto]"  # encrypted entries
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[zstd]"    # zstd compression before Python 3.14
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[casbin]"  # authorization with Casbin
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-jwt]"     # JWTStrategy
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-oauth2]"  # OAuth2Strategy
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-saml]"    # SAMLStrategy

Python 3.11+, FastAPI 0.115+ and Pydantic v2.

docs.title: The app
docs.text:
An app as it runs in production: its configuration from the environment, the cache in Redis, shared by every process, and its entries signed.

from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Header
from pydantic import BaseModel, SecretStr
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict
from redis import asyncio as aioredis

from fastapi_alcazaba import FastAPICache
from fastapi_alcazaba.backends.redis import RedisBackend
from fastapi_alcazaba.response_cache import cache


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    """From environment variables (REDIS_URL...) or a .env file."""

    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env", env_file_encoding="utf-8")

    redis_url: str
    cache_signing_key: SecretStr  # secrets.token_urlsafe(32)


settings = Settings()


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(_: FastAPI) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    redis = aioredis.from_url(settings.redis_url)
    FastAPICache.init(RedisBackend(redis), prefix="myapp", signing_key=settings.cache_signing_key)
    yield
    await redis.aclose()


app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)


class Product(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float


def current_user(authorization: str = Header()) -> str:
    return authorization  # validate the token here


@app.get("/products/{product_id}")
@cache(expire=60, vary_headers=())  # same response for everybody: one shared entry
async def product(product_id: int) -> Product:
    return Product(name="Olive oil", price=9.5)


@app.get("/me")
@cache(expire=30)  # one entry per Authorization/Cookie value, sent as private
async def me(user: str = Depends(current_user)) -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"user": user}

@cache goes between the route decorator and the function. It also caches plain functions, sync or async (sync ones run in the thread pool, like FastAPI does).

The configuration comes from pydantic-settings (pip install pydantic-settings). Every parameter that takes a key or a secret also takes pydantic's SecretStr (or SecretBytes) as it is, so the value stays out of the settings' repr and of tracebacks until Alcazaba uses it. The other snippets read theirs from the same settings.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Backends: Redis, Valkey, GLIDE, memcached, DynamoDB, and a copy in each process in front of them.
  • Security model and resilience: what gets cached and for whom, what the backend is trusted with, and what happens when it fails.
  • Metrics and traces: what Alcazaba records with OpenTelemetry, and the logs to configure.

docs.title: Security model and resilience
docs.text:
What the cache stores and for whom, what it trusts the backend with, and what happens when the backend fails.

Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text:
• What gets cached: GET requests (any call for plain functions) whose response is a 200 and doesn't say Cache-Control: no-store.
  • Per-user data: requests are told apart by the endpoint's arguments plus the vary_headers. If a response depends on anything else (request.state, a header that isn't in vary_headers, the client IP…), add it to vary_headers or to a custom key builder.
  • The backend is trusted for availability, not for integrity: without a signing_key or an encryption_key, whoever can write to it decides what your endpoints return. Use one whenever the backend is shared or reachable by others, and always with PickleCoder.
  • Confidentiality: signed entries are readable by whoever can read the backend, its dumps (RDB/AOF files) and backups. When responses carry personal or sensitive data, use encryption_key instead.
  • Keys built by the default key builder are SHA-256 digests: arguments and tokens never appear in the backend in clear text.
  • Fail open: if the backend is down or an entry can't be decoded, the endpoint runs as if there were no cache. Rate limiters let requests through too, unless fail_open=False.
  • Rate limits count clients by the address the ASGI server gives, IPv6 by /64 (configure it to trust your proxy, and only it), or by your identifier. Whoever can write to the backend can reset them; clear() can't.

Report vulnerabilities as described in SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Resilience
docs.text:
The cache never makes a request fail. Every backend call has a timeout (backend_timeout, 1 s by default): if it runs out, or the backend fails, the request goes on without cache. After circuit_breaker_failures consecutive failures the backend isn't called at all for circuit_breaker_reset seconds, so that requests don't each wait for the timeout; then one call tries again.

Concurrent misses for the same key compute once per process (single_flight). With several processes or containers, distributed_lock=True makes the first one take a lock in Redis/Valkey while the others wait for its value (up to lock_wait seconds). And early_refresh=0.1 lets callers refresh an entry, with growing probability, during the last 10 % of its lifetime: popular entries are renewed before they expire, instead of every caller missing at once. If that refresh fails, the cached value is served.

docs.title: Checking uploads
docs.text:
In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

The name and the Content-Type of an upload are whatever the client chose: an HTML page sent as cat.png would be served back as HTML. FastAPIUploads checks the file itself, with nothing but the standard library:

from fastapi_alcazaba.uploads import IMAGES, CheckedFile, FastAPIUploads

uploads = FastAPIUploads(types=IMAGES, max_size=5 * 1024 * 1024, max_pixels=25_000_000)


@app.post("/avatars")
async def avatar(upload: Annotated[CheckedFile, Depends(uploads)]) -> dict[str, str]:
    name = f"{uuid4()}{upload.extension}"  # never the client's name
    await storage.save(name, upload.file.file, content_type=upload.content_type)
    return {"name": name}

As a dependency it reads the form field file; for other fields or several files, call await uploads.check(file). It returns a CheckedFile: the UploadFile read back to its start, the content_type found in its bytes, its size, its width and height (images) and a safe filename.

  • The real type (sniff(data)): PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, PDF, ZIP, GZIP, MP4 and QuickTime from their signatures; Word, Excel and PowerPoint documents from the content types their [Content_Types].xml declares (as Office reads them), with the macro-enabled ones (.docm, .xlsm, .pptm) told apart, and anything ambiguous reported as a plain ZIP; UTF-8 text without control characters (text/plain: CSV is text, it can't be told apart). Text that starts with a tag is HTML, SVG or XML, never plain text, and SVG is never an image: all three can carry scripts. types must come from KNOWN_TYPES (IMAGES, OFFICE_DOCUMENTS...), so a typo like image/jpg fails at start-up. Store and serve files with the detected type, never the client's, plus X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff (SecurityHeadersMiddleware).
  • Size: counted while the file is read in chunks, whatever UploadFile.size says; 413 beyond max_size, 415 for a type that isn't allowed, 422 for an empty file. By the time an endpoint runs the multipart parser has stored the whole request already, so limit it with BodySizeLimitMiddleware on the route as well.
  • Decompression bombs: the width and height of PNG, JPEG (however much metadata comes before the frame), GIF and WebP images are read from their headers (image_size(data)) without decoding them; more than max_pixels (40 million by default) gets a 413, and an image whose dimensions can't be read a 415.
  • Safe names (safe_filename(name)): NFKC-normalised, only the last path component, without control or invisible characters (such as the right-to-left override that shows exe.txt as txt.exe), <>:"|?* replaced, without leading dots or dashes, _ in front of the names Windows reserves (CON, NUL, COM1...), and at most 255 bytes, keeping the extension. For display and Content-Disposition; store files under names of your own (CheckedFile.extension).
  • What it doesn't do: look inside the files. A PDF can carry scripts, Office documents macros, archives may expand to far more than their size, and the frames of a GIF aren't counted. Allow HTML, SVG or XML only to serve them as attachments from another domain.

docs.title: Webhooks and outbound calls
docs.text:
Webhooks signed and verified the Standard Webhooks way, and calls to other services with a deadline, a circuit breaker and SSRF protection.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Signed webhooks
docs.text:
FastAPIWebhooks accepts only webhooks signed with your secret, and each delivery once. WebhookSigner signs the ones you send. Both follow Standard Webhooks, the format of Svix, Supabase, Clerk, Resend, OpenAI and others: webhook-id, webhook-timestamp and webhook-signature: v1,<base64 HMAC-SHA256 of "id.timestamp.body">, with whsec_... secrets.

from fastapi_alcazaba.webhooks import FastAPIWebhooks, WebhookMessage, WebhookSigner

webhooks = FastAPIWebhooks(settings.webhook_secret)  # "whsec_..."


@app.post("/webhooks/payments")
async def payment_event(message: Annotated[WebhookMessage, Depends(webhooks)]) -> None:
    event = message.json()
    ...  # idempotent on message.id: retries of a message keep its id


# Sending them: sign the exact bytes you send.
signer = WebhookSigner(settings.webhook_secret)  # WebhookSigner.generate_secret() makes one
body = json.dumps(event).encode()
await client.post(url, content=body, headers=signer.sign(body))
  • Raw body, still readable: the signature is checked over the body exactly as it arrived, read up to max_body_size bytes (1 MiB; a 413 beyond, and a Content-Length over it is refused before reading). It stays in the request, for message.json() or await request.json(). Validate it with your model there (Event.model_validate_json(message.body)) rather than with a pydantic body parameter: FastAPI reads and validates those before any dependency runs, so the body would be read without the limit, and an unsigned malformed one would get a 422 before its signature is checked. Not a form parameter either, which consumes the body first.
  • Freshness: a timestamp more than tolerance seconds (300) away from the server's clock, in the past or the future, is refused.
  • Constant time, one answer: every signature in the header is compared in constant time against each secret. A wrong signature, a stale timestamp and a replay all get the same 401 ("Invalid webhook"); only missing or malformed headers get a 400.
  • Replays: each accepted delivery (its id and timestamp, as a SHA-256 digest under Cache.state_key) is counted in the cache's backend until its timestamp can't be accepted anymore, so a captured request sent again is refused by every process. Only accepted deliveries are counted: a forged copy can't burn the id of the real one. A retry of the sender has a new timestamp and signature and goes through, as it must after a failed attempt: make the endpoint idempotent on message.id (a unique constraint) if a message must not be processed twice. The backend must support counters, as every built-in backend does.
  • Backend down: a 503 with Retry-After (fail closed): senders retry later, while a replay would run its effects again. fail_open=True accepts correctly signed webhooks without the replay check instead.
  • Rotation: FastAPIWebhooks([new, old]) accepts a signature by either secret; WebhookSigner([new, old]) signs every message with both, so receivers with either secret accept it.
  • Without a dependency: webhooks.verify(headers, body) checks the signature and the timestamp (not replays), for queues and scripts.

docs.title: Outbound calls
docs.text:
ResilientTransport is an httpx transport for the calls your app makes to other services: a deadline for each call and a circuit breaker for each origin. It needs httpx2 (or httpx):

import httpx2 as httpx

from fastapi_alcazaba.outbound import CircuitOpenError, ResilientTransport


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    transport = ResilientTransport(timeout=5, failure_threshold=5, reset_timeout=30)
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=transport, base_url="https://api.example.com") as client:
        app.state.partner_api = client
        yield


@app.get("/quote")
async def quote(request: Request) -> Quote:
    try:
        response = await request.app.state.partner_api.get("/quote")
    except CircuitOpenError:  # the service keeps failing: don't wait for it
        raise HTTPException(503, "Quotes are unavailable, try again later")
    return Quote.model_validate(response.json())
  • Deadline: timeout bounds the whole call, from sending the request to the last byte of the response. httpx's own timeouts are per phase, and its read timeout restarts with every byte, so a server that trickles a byte every few seconds would keep the request open forever. Past the deadline, httpx.TimeoutException. It applies to each request the transport sends: with follow_redirects=True, every hop gets a deadline of its own.
  • Response size: responses are read whole before they're returned, so don't stream large downloads through it. max_response_size caps the bytes read (as received, before decompression); past it, ResponseTooLargeError, an httpx.RequestError.
  • Circuit breaker: each origin (scheme, host and port) has its own. After failure_threshold consecutive failures, calls to that origin fail at once with CircuitOpenError for reset_timeout seconds, without reaching the server; then a single trial call decides whether it's back. CircuitOpenError is an httpx.TransportError, so code that already handles httpx errors handles it too. transport.state(url) says "closed", "open" or "half-open", handy in a health check. failure_threshold=None turns it off.
  • What counts as a failure: the origin's transport errors (connection and protocol errors, timeouts, yours and httpx's) and responses whose status is in failure_statuses (500, 502, 503 and 504 by default), which are still returned to you. Any other response, 4xx included, is a success. Your own errors are neither: an illegal header value (httpx.LocalProtocolError), a URL scheme httpx can't send (httpx.UnsupportedProtocol), an exception from your request body, ResponseTooLargeError. Otherwise anyone who can put a string in an outbound header could switch the integration off for everybody.
  • Your own transport settings: ResilientTransport(httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport(verify=..., limits=..., proxy=...)).

docs.title: URLs your users give: SSRF
docs.text:
Calling a URL that a user typed (a webhook endpoint, a link preview, an avatar by URL) lets them make your server call its own network: http://169.254.169.254/ (the cloud's metadata service and its credentials), http://localhost:6379/, an admin panel on 10.0.0.0/8. SSRFGuardTransport only calls the public internet:

from fastapi_alcazaba.outbound import (
    BlockedDestinationError,
    ResilientTransport,
    SSRFGuardTransport,
)

client = httpx.AsyncClient(
    transport=ResilientTransport(SSRFGuardTransport(ports=(443,)), timeout=10),
    follow_redirects=True,
)

try:
    await client.post(subscription.url, content=body, headers=signer.sign(body))
except BlockedDestinationError:
    ...  # tell the user the URL isn't allowed
  • What's refused: a host with any address that isn't public: private, loopback, link-local (169.254.0.0/16 and its metadata services, fe80::/10), carrier-grade NAT (100.64.0.0/10), multicast, reserved, documentation and benchmarking ranges, unique-local IPv6 (fc00::/7, AWS's fd00:ec2::254), and the IPv6 forms of those IPv4 addresses (::ffff:127.0.0.1, NAT64 64:ff9b::/96, 6to4, Teredo). Literal addresses in URLs are checked without DNS; anything else goes to DNS, so numeric spellings (http://2130706433/, http://0x7f.1/) and localhost are refused for what they resolve to. Also refused: schemes other than http and https and, with ports, other ports. BlockedDestinationError says which host, never the address it resolved to (that's logged instead).
  • Pinned against DNS rebinding: the transport resolves the host itself and connects to the address it checked: the URL is rewritten to it, the Host header keeps the name, and TLS gets the name for SNI and the certificate check. A DNS server that answers a public address to the check and a private one to the connection gets nowhere. If the first address can't be reached, one of the other family (IPv4/IPv6) is tried.
  • Redirects: with follow_redirects=True, every hop goes through the transport and is checked like the first one.
  • Checking a URL when it's given: await guard.check(url) checks it as a request would be (scheme, port, every address its host resolves to) without sending anything, so a webhook's endpoint can be refused when a user registers it. Each request is checked again all the same: DNS answers change.
  • Allowed internal destinations: allow=["billing.internal", "*.svc.cluster.local", "10.1.2.0/24"] lets those names (exact, or subdomains) and networks through although they aren't public; they're still pinned.
  • With ResilientTransport: wrap the guard in it (not the other way round): the deadline then covers the DNS lookup and each breaker is per host name. BlockedDestinationError is an httpx.RequestError but not a TransportError, so it doesn't count against the origin's breaker or trigger retry policies.
  • Connections: each host name gets an httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport of its own (sharing one SSL context), at most max_hosts (100) kept open: pinned connections are pooled by address, and two names on one address (a CDN) must not share a connection whose certificate was checked for the other. Pass a factory for your own settings, SSRFGuardTransport(lambda: httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport(http2=True)), or a transport instance (a mock in tests), which then carries every request.
  • Proxies: a proxy connects on its own, so pinning can't work through it: httpx.AsyncHTTPTransport(proxy=...) as the inner transport is refused. Don't pass proxy= or mounts= to the client either: those requests would bypass the transport. (The client ignores the HTTP_PROXY variables when it's given a transport.) An egress proxy that filters destinations itself, such as Smokescreen, is the alternative.

docs.title: Authentication strategies
docs.text:
Who makes a request, told by strategies: JWTs, bearer tokens, sessions, logins with GitHub or any OAuth2 provider, single sign-on with a SAML identity provider, or your own.

In an app: the example. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Strategies
docs.text:
FastAPIAuth tells who makes a request by strategies: each strategy knows one way (a JWT, a session, a login with GitHub…), and a dependency tries those of a route in order. The first one that finds a user gives it to the route; when none does, a 401. Each strategy has its extra:

pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-jwt]"          # JWTStrategy, with PyJWT
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-oauth2]"       # OAuth2Strategy, with httpx2
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-saml]"         # SAMLStrategy, with signxml
pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-http-bearer]"  # HTTPBearerStrategy: nothing more

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth import FastAPIAuth, SessionStrategy
from fastapi_alcazaba.auth.strategies.jwt import JWTStrategy
from fastapi_alcazaba.auth.strategies.oauth2 import OAuth2Strategy

auth = FastAPIAuth()
github = auth.use(
    OAuth2Strategy(
        name="github",
        authorization_url="https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize",
        token_url="https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token",
        userinfo_url="https://api.github.com/user",
        client_id=settings.github_client_id,
        client_secret=settings.github_client_secret,
        redirect_uri="https://example.com/auth/github/callback",
        verify=find_or_create_user,  # (tokens, profile) -> your user
    )
)
sessions = auth.use(SessionStrategy(load_user))  # load_user(user_id) -> your user
tokens = auth.use(JWTStrategy(settings.jwt_secret, verify=lambda c: load_user(c["sub"])))

CurrentUser = Annotated[User, Depends(auth.authenticate("session", "jwt"))]
GitHubUser = Annotated[User, Depends(auth.authenticate("github"))]


@app.get("/me")
async def me(user: CurrentUser) -> User:  # a browser's session, or a script's token
    return user


@app.get("/login/github")
async def login() -> RedirectResponse:
    return github.redirect()  # to GitHub, which sends the user back to the callback


@app.get("/auth/github/callback")
async def callback(request: Request, user: GitHubUser) -> RedirectResponse:
    sessions.login(request, user.id)
    return RedirectResponse("/me", status_code=303)

The strategies of a dependency are tried in order. Each returns the user; None when the request doesn't carry its credentials; or raises AuthenticationFailed when they're there but wrong (logged, never sent). Either way the next one is tried. When none finds a user, a 401 with the WWW-Authenticate challenges of those tried, a WebSocket is closed with 1008, and optional=True gives None. Any other error is a 500, never a request let through. Without a dependency: await auth.user(connection). The verify and load_user functions that turn credentials into your user can be async or not, and return None to refuse them.

Each strategy has its page:

  • JWTStrategy: JWTs, the app's own or an identity provider's.
  • OAuth2Strategy: logins with GitHub, Google or any OAuth2 or OpenID Connect provider.
  • SessionStrategy: the user kept in the session at login.
  • HTTPBearerStrategy: opaque bearer tokens that your function looks up.
  • SAMLStrategy: single sign-on with a SAML identity provider.
  • Your own strategy: an API key, a client certificate, a signed request…

docs.title: HTTPBearerStrategy
docs.text:
Opaque bearer tokens that your function looks up: pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-http-bearer]", which installs nothing more.

In an app: the example. How strategies are tried: Strategies. Every argument: the API reference.

HTTPBearerStrategy takes opaque tokens of Authorization: Bearer, which your verify(token) looks up (in a database, at the provider's introspection endpoint). It needs no other library.

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth import HTTPBearerStrategy


async def find_token(token: str) -> User | None:
    digest = hashlib.sha256(token.encode()).hexdigest()  # store digests, not tokens
    return await db.user_by_token_digest(digest)


bearer = auth.use(HTTPBearerStrategy(find_token))

A token that isn't RFC 6750's syntax, or longer than 4 KiB, fails without reaching verify. Keep digests of the tokens, not the tokens. Behind a JWTStrategy, JWTs go to that one and opaque tokens to this one.

docs.title: JWTStrategy
docs.text:
JWTs, the app's own or an identity provider's: pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-jwt]".

In an app: the example. How strategies are tried: Strategies. Every argument: the API reference.

JWTStrategy reads the token of Authorization: Bearer (or of the cookie named by cookie=) and verifies it with PyJWT: the signature, exp, nbf and the required claims (exp, sub), and aud and iss when given; a token with an aud is refused when no audience is set, as it's meant for another service. alg: none never, nor HMAC and asymmetric algorithms together: a public key taken for an HMAC secret would let anyone sign.

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth import TokenBlocklist
from fastapi_alcazaba.auth.strategies.jwt import JWTStrategy

# The app's own tokens, signed with the first secret; the second one still verifies.
tokens = auth.use(
    JWTStrategy(
        [settings.jwt_secret, settings.previous_jwt_secret],
        verify=lambda claims: load_user(claims["sub"]),
        blocklist=TokenBlocklist(),
    )
)
token = tokens.issue(str(user.id), expires_in=900)

# An identity provider's tokens, with its public keys.
idp = auth.use(
    JWTStrategy(
        jwks_url="https://idp.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json",
        algorithms=["RS256"],
        audience="https://api.example.com",
        issuer="https://idp.example.com/",
        name="idp",
    )
)
  • Keys: HMAC secrets have at least 32 bytes and rotate with a list; public keys need algorithms=["RS256"] (or ES256, EdDSA…), and an identity provider's keys come from its JWKS (jwks_url=, by each token's kid), with the audience and issuer it requires: a provider signs the tokens of every app it serves with the same keys.
  • Revoked tokens: blocklist= refuses the tokens revoked in a TokenBlocklist (see "Revoked tokens and one-time codes").
  • Issuing: issue(subject, expires_in=900) signs one, with iat, exp and a random jti.
  • OpenAPI: it shows in the schema, for the docs' Authorize button.

docs.title: OAuth2Strategy
docs.text:
Logins with GitHub, Google or any OAuth2 or OpenID Connect provider: pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-oauth2]".

In an app: the example. How strategies are tried, and the code of a login with GitHub: Strategies. Every argument: the API reference.

OAuth2Strategy logs people in with the authorization code flow and PKCE, for any OAuth2 or OpenID Connect provider (GitHub, Google, Keycloak…):

  • The login: redirect() sends the browser to the provider with a random state; the state and the PKCE verifier wait in a cookie for 10 minutes (__Host-, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax).
  • The callback: the strategy checks the state, so that nobody can log a user in with their own account (login CSRF); exchanges the code, with the app's credentials by HTTP Basic (client_auth="post" in the form); reads userinfo_url; and calls verify(tokens, profile). It only goes on the callback route: elsewhere it finds nobody.
  • The provider: its URLs are HTTPS (or http://localhost); a provider that doesn't answer is a 502.

docs.title: SAMLStrategy
docs.text:
Single sign-on with a SAML identity provider: pip install "fastapi-alcazaba[auth-strategy-saml]".

In an app: the example. How strategies are tried: Strategies. Every argument: the API reference.

SAMLStrategy is SAML 2.0 single sign-on with an identity provider (Okta, Entra ID, ADFS, Keycloak…):

  • The login: redirect() sends the browser to the IdP with an AuthnRequest; the IdP posts its answer to the ACS route.
  • The answer: the strategy verifies its XML signature with the IdP's certificate (signxml, SHA-2 only, no DTDs). Then, on what the signature covers and nothing else (signature wrapping), it checks the issuer, the audience (entity_id), the recipient (acs_url), the request it answers and when it's valid.
  • Once: each assertion works once: it's kept in the cache's backend until it expires, and logins are refused when the backend fails.
  • Metadata: metadata() is the app's metadata, for the IdP.
  • Not supported: logins the IdP starts, encrypted assertions, signed requests, single logout.

The SAML request's id waits in a SameSite=None cookie, because the IdP posts the answer from its own site; for the same reason CSRFMiddleware must let the ACS through:

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth.strategies.saml import SAMLStrategy

saml = auth.use(
    SAMLStrategy(
        entity_id="https://example.com/saml/metadata",  # this app, at the IdP
        acs_url="https://example.com/saml/acs",
        idp_entity_id=settings.idp_entity_id,
        idp_sso_url=settings.idp_sso_url,
        idp_certificate=settings.idp_certificate,  # PEM; a list while it rotates
        verify=find_or_create_user,  # (SAMLProfile) -> your user
    )
)
SAMLUser = Annotated[User, Depends(auth.authenticate("saml"))]
app.add_middleware(CSRFMiddleware, exempt_paths=["/saml/acs"])  # the IdP posts it


@app.get("/saml/login")
async def saml_login() -> RedirectResponse:
    return saml.redirect()


@app.post("/saml/acs")
async def saml_acs(request: Request, user: SAMLUser) -> RedirectResponse:
    sessions.login(request, user.id)
    return RedirectResponse("/me", status_code=303)


@app.get("/saml/metadata")
async def saml_metadata() -> Response:
    return Response(saml.metadata(), media_type="application/samlmetadata+xml")

docs.title: SessionStrategy
docs.text:
The user kept in the session at login, for the browsers of an app's users.

In an app: the example. How strategies are tried, and the code of a login that starts a session: Strategies. The sessions themselves: Sessions, CSRF and security headers. Every argument: the API reference.

SessionStrategy finds the user id that sessions.login(request, user_id) kept in the session, and loads the user with load_user. With ServerSessionMiddleware the session gets a new id at login (no session fixation), and sessions.logout(request) deletes it from the backend. A session whose user doesn't exist any more fails.

docs.title: Your own strategy
docs.text:
An API key, a client certificate, a signed request…: any way to tell who makes a request.

In an app: the example. How strategies are tried: Strategies. Every argument: the API reference.

Your own strategy (an API key, a client certificate, a signed request…) is a Strategy whose authenticate() returns the user, None, or raises AuthenticationFailed; challenge and openapi_scheme() are optional:

from fastapi import HTTPException
from starlette.requests import HTTPConnection

from fastapi_alcazaba.auth import AuthenticationFailed, FastAPIAPIKeys, Strategy


class APIKeyStrategy(Strategy):
    challenge = "APIKey"

    def __init__(self, keys: FastAPIAPIKeys[Any]) -> None:
        super().__init__("api-key")
        self.keys = keys

    async def authenticate(self, connection: HTTPConnection) -> Any:
        key = connection.headers.get("x-api-key")
        if key is None:
            return None  # not this strategy's: the next one is tried
        try:
            return await self.keys.authenticate(key)
        except HTTPException as exc:  # FastAPIAPIKeys' 401
            raise AuthenticationFailed("invalid API key") from exc


auth.use(APIKeyStrategy(keys))

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text: In an app: the examples. Every class and function: the API reference.

docs.title: Strategies
docs.text:
Twelve strategies, with nothing but FastAPI and pydantic. Each is configured once and used as a dependency, which reads and checks its query parameters; the endpoint gets them as an argument, so @cache keeps each page under a key of its own:

Strategy Query parameters For PaginationPageNumber page, page_size Numbered pages, with the total PaginationLimitOffset limit, offset Slices, with the total PaginationOffset offset, limit Slices, without counting the whole list PaginationRange start, end Ranges of items, with Content-Range PaginationCursor cursor, limit An opaque, signed cursor: infinite scroll, feeds PaginationKeyset after, before, limit Keyset pagination, both ways PaginationIdBased last_id, limit The id of the last item seen PaginationTimeBased timestamp, limit Before or after a time: feeds, syncing PaginationSearchAfter search_after, limit The sort values of the last item, readable PaginationToken page_token, page_size An opaque token, bound to the query, that expires PaginationScroll scroll_id, batch_size A snapshot kept in the backend, read in batches PaginationStreaming none Every item as it comes, as NDJSON 
from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.page_number import (
    PageNumberPage,
    PageNumberParams,
    PaginationPageNumber,
)

pages = PaginationPageNumber(default_page_size=20, max_page_size=100)


@app.get("/products")
@cache(expire=60, tags=["products"])
async def products(
    params: Annotated[PageNumberParams, Depends(pages)],
) -> PageNumberPage[Product]:
    return pages.paginate(await load_products(), params)
  • By position or by key: page numbers, offsets and ranges count items, so a row added or deleted meanwhile shifts the pages (an item skipped or seen twice), and a database walks past every row before the page. Cursors, keysets, ids, timestamps and sort values point at the last item instead: the pages don't shift, and an index finds any of them as fast as the first.
  • Links: the response links to the pages around it in the Link header (RFC 8288), as GitHub's API does: </products?page=3&page_size=20>; rel="next". The links keep the request's other query parameters and leave out the host, so they don't depend on the Host header nor on a proxy in front. Pages served from the cache get them too, made for the request they answer.
  • From a database: paginate takes the whole list and finds the page in it, or the rows the database returned for the page: with their total for the strategies that count, or queried=True for the others, which fetch one row more (params.fetch) to tell whether there's a next page.
  • Limits: each strategy has its own maximum (100 items by default), so that nobody asks for a million rows at once: anything beyond, or malformed, is a 422 before the endpoint runs. They're in the OpenAPI schema too.
  • Cached: every page, size and filter is one entry: tag them (tags=["products"]) to drop them all when the data changes. For short lists, caching the whole list with get_or_set and slicing every page from it keeps a single entry. The pagination example does it three ways, with the database session left out of the key (exclude_params).

Each strategy has its page:

  • PaginationPageNumber: numbered pages, with the total: ?page=2&page_size=20.
  • PaginationLimitOffset: slices, with the total: ?limit=20&offset=40.
  • PaginationOffset: slices without counting the whole list: ?offset=40&limit=20.
  • PaginationRange: ranges of items, with Content-Range: ?start=0&end=24.
  • PaginationCursor: an opaque, signed cursor: ?limit=20&cursor=....
  • PaginationKeyset: keyset pagination, both ways: ?after=... or ?before=....
  • PaginationIdBased: the id of the last item seen: ?last_id=42&limit=20.
  • PaginationTimeBased: before or after a time: ?timestamp=2026-10-29T10:00:00Z&limit=20.
  • PaginationSearchAfter: the sort values of the last item: ?search_after=["...",42]&limit=20.
  • PaginationToken: an opaque token, bound to the query, that expires: ?page_token=...&page_size=20.
  • PaginationScroll: a snapshot kept in the backend, read in batches: ?scroll_id=....
  • PaginationStreaming: every item as it comes, as NDJSON, without pages.

docs.title: PaginationCursor
docs.text:
An opaque, signed cursor: ?limit=20&cursor=....

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

A cursor points at the last item of a page by its sort key, not by its position: rows added or deleted meanwhile don't shift the pages (no item skipped or seen twice), and a database finds any page through an index, as fast as the first. For infinite scroll, feeds and clients that sync everything:

from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.cursor import CursorPage, CursorParams, PaginationCursor

cursors = PaginationCursor(secret=settings.cursor_secret)  # secrets.token_urlsafe(32)


@app.get("/events")
@cache(expire=60)
async def events(params: Annotated[CursorParams, Depends(cursors)]) -> CursorPage[Event]:
    query = select(Event).order_by(Event.created_at, Event.id).limit(params.fetch)
    if params.after is not None:  # (created_at, id) of the last event seen
        query = query.where(tuple_(Event.created_at, Event.id) > params.after)
    rows = (await session.scalars(query)).all()
    return cursors.paginate(rows, params, key=lambda e: (e.created_at, e.id), queried=True)

GET /events?limit=20 answers {"items": [...], "limit": 20, "next_cursor": "WyIyMDI2..."}, and ?cursor=<next_cursor> the next page; next_cursor is null on the last one. The Link header has the first page and, except on the last page, the next one.

  • The sort key (key) must be unique: (created_at, id), not created_at alone, which two items may share. Its values can be strings, integers (up to 64 bits), floats, booleans, datetimes, dates, UUIDs and decimals, and params.after has them back as such.
  • Queried or sliced: with queried=True, the rows are those of the page, queried with a key past params.after and params.fetch (one more than limit: it tells whether there's a next page). Without it, paginate finds the page in the whole sorted list. descending=True for newest first.
  • Signed: with a secret, cursors carry an HMAC-SHA256 and a client can't make one up or change it; a list rotates secrets. Without it, a cursor's values are checked to be of those types. Either way an invalid cursor is a 400, and one longer than 1024 characters or malformed a 422, before the endpoint runs. Cursors are base64, not encrypted: clients can read the sort key, so sort by what they may see.
  • Forward only: to go back, clients keep the cursors they've used, or use PaginationKeyset, which goes both ways.

docs.title: PaginationIdBased
docs.text:
The id of the last item seen: ?last_id=42&limit=20.

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

The items after the last one seen, by id: GET /messages?last_id=42&limit=20 answers {"items": [...], "limit": 20, "last_id": 62, "has_more": true}, and ?last_id=62 the next page. The id travels as it is, neither encoded nor signed, since ids are public: a client that keeps the last one it has asks for whatever came after it. Rows added or deleted meanwhile don't shift the pages, and the primary key finds any page as fast as the first. For syncing, chats, and lists sorted by id:

from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.id_based import IdBasedPage, IdBasedParams, PaginationIdBased

ids = PaginationIdBased(default_limit=20, max_limit=100)  # PaginationIdBased(UUID) for UUIDs


@app.get("/messages")
@cache(expire=60, tags=["messages"])
async def messages(params: Annotated[IdBasedParams, Depends(ids)]) -> IdBasedPage[Message]:
    query = select(Message).order_by(Message.id).limit(params.fetch)
    if params.last_id is not None:
        query = query.where(Message.id > params.last_id)
    rows = (await session.scalars(query)).all()
    return ids.paginate(rows, params, key=lambda m: m.id, queried=True)
  • The id's type: int by default, or str or UUID (PaginationIdBased(UUID)), which is the query parameter's type: a last_id of another type is a 422, and integers are kept to 64 bits, as databases store them. The ids must be unique, and sort as the database sorts them.
  • Queried or sliced: with queried=True, the rows are those of WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT :fetch, one more than limit when there's a next page. Without it, paginate finds the page in the whole list, sorted by id. descending=True for newest first: the next page holds the ids smaller than last_id (WHERE id < :last_id ORDER BY id DESC).
  • last_id and has_more: last_id is the id of the page's last item, null when it's empty (a client that has caught up keeps its own); has_more says whether there's a next page. The Link header has the first page and, while has_more, the next one.
  • Forward only, by one column: to go back, clients keep the ids they've used. To sort by other columns, or by several, or to keep the sort key from clients, use PaginationCursor, whose cursors are opaque and can be signed.

docs.title: PaginationKeyset
docs.text:
Keyset pagination, both ways: ?after=... or ?before=....

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

Keyset pagination in both directions: ?after=<after> gives the page after a key and ?before=<before> the page before one, a key being the sort key of the item at the edge of a page. Each page is a query through an index, from either side, as fast on the last page as on the first, and rows added or deleted meanwhile don't shift the pages. For lists with "Previous" and "Next", and histories scrolled both ways:

from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.keyset import KeysetPage, KeysetParams, PaginationKeyset

keyset = PaginationKeyset(secret=settings.keyset_secret)  # secrets.token_urlsafe(32)


@app.get("/products")
@cache(expire=60, tags=["products"])
async def products(params: Annotated[KeysetParams, Depends(keyset)]) -> KeysetPage[Product]:
    key = tuple_(Product.price, Product.id)
    if params.before is not None:  # the page before: the nearest rows first
        query = select(Product).where(key < params.before)
        query = query.order_by(Product.price.desc(), Product.id.desc())
    else:
        query = select(Product).order_by(Product.price, Product.id)
        if params.after is not None:
            query = query.where(key > params.after)
    rows = (await session.scalars(query.limit(params.fetch))).all()
    return keyset.paginate(rows, params, key=lambda p: (p.price, p.id), queried=True)

GET /products?limit=20 answers {"items": [...], "limit": 20, "before": null, "after": "WzQuMiwxMl0..."}: after is the key of the last item (null on the last page), and before the key of the first (null on the first page). The Link header has the first page and, when there's one, the page before (before=...) and the next (after=...).

  • The key must be unique: (price, id), not price alone, which two items may share. Its values can be strings, integers (up to 64 bits), floats, booleans, datetimes, dates, UUIDs and decimals, and params.after and params.before have them back as such.
  • Queried or sliced: with queried=True, the rows are those the database returned, up to params.fetch (the limit and one more, which tells whether there's another page that way): past params.after in order, or with params.before, before it in the reverse order, nearest first, which paginate puts back in order. The other way there's always a page, the one the key came from. Without it, paginate finds the page in the whole sorted list. descending=True for newest first, where after reads key < :after and before key > :before ORDER BY key.
  • Signed: with a secret, keys carry an HMAC-SHA256 and a client can't make one up or change it; a list rotates secrets. An invalid key is a 400 (Invalid after, Invalid before), and so are after and before together. Keys are base64, not encrypted: clients can read the sort key, so sort by what they may see.
  • Limits: no total and no page numbers, only the first, previous and next pages. Going back from a page that didn't start where the first page's walk would have, the first page can be shorter than the limit.

docs.title: PaginationLimitOffset
docs.text:
Slices, with the total: ?limit=20&offset=40.

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

Slices, with the total: GET /products?limit=20&offset=40 answers {"items": [...], "total": 245, "limit": 20, "offset": 40}. The same as page numbers for clients that count in items rather than pages, and can ask for any slice.

from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.limit_offset import (
    LimitOffsetPage,
    LimitOffsetParams,
    PaginationLimitOffset,
)

slices = PaginationLimitOffset(default_limit=20, max_limit=100)


@app.get("/products")
async def products(
    params: Annotated[LimitOffsetParams, Depends(slices)],
) -> LimitOffsetPage[Product]:
    rows = await session.scalars(select(Product).limit(params.limit).offset(params.offset))
    return slices.paginate(rows.all(), params, total=await count_products())
  • Links: first, previous, next and last, on the grid of limit from 0, where clients that start at the first page walk.
  • Without the total: PaginationOffset skips the count.

docs.title: PaginationOffset
docs.text:
Slices without counting the whole list: ?offset=40&limit=20.

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

Slices without the total: GET /logs?offset=40&limit=20 answers {"items": [...], "offset": 40, "limit": 20, "has_more": true}. The database is asked for one row more than the page (params.fetch), which isn't returned but tells whether there's a next one, so the list is never counted. For lists whose count is slow (big tables, searches, joins) or outdated as soon as it's made, and for clients that only ever go to the next page:

from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.offset import OffsetPage, OffsetParams, PaginationOffset

offsets = PaginationOffset(default_limit=20, max_limit=100)


@app.get("/logs")
@cache(expire=10)
async def logs(params: Annotated[OffsetParams, Depends(offsets)]) -> OffsetPage[Line]:
    query = select(Line).order_by(Line.id.desc()).limit(params.fetch).offset(params.offset)
    rows = (await session.scalars(query)).all()
    return offsets.paginate(rows, params, queried=True)
  • Queried or sliced: with queried=True, the rows are those of LIMIT params.fetch OFFSET params.offset, one more than limit when there's a next page. Without it, paginate slices the page from the whole list.
  • Links: first, previous and, while has_more, next. There's no last page, nor a number of pages: for those, PaginationLimitOffset counts.
  • By position: a row added or deleted before the page shifts it, so an item may be skipped or seen twice, and a database still walks past every row before the offset: deep pages get slower. For lists that grow while they're read, page by key (PaginationIdBased, PaginationCursor).
  • Limits: limit up to max_limit and offset from 0, a 422 otherwise.

docs.title: PaginationPageNumber
docs.text:
Numbered pages, with the total: ?page=2&page_size=20.

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

Numbered pages, with the total: GET /products?page=2&page_size=20 answers {"items": [...], "total": 245, "page": 2, "page_size": 20, "pages": 13}. For lists that people browse page by page, jump through, and want to know the size of.

  • From a database: query only the page, with params.offset and params.limit, and count: pages.paginate(rows, params, total=count). Without total, paginate slices the page from the whole list.
  • Links: first, previous, next and last.
  • Its cost: counting the whole list on every page, and the shifting of pages by position.

docs.title: PaginationRange
docs.text:
Ranges of items, with Content-Range: ?start=0&end=24.

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

Ranges of items by the indexes of the first and the last, from 0 and both included: GET /contacts?start=0&end=24 answers {"items": [...], "start": 0, "end": 24, "total": 319, "limit": 25} with Content-Range: items 0-24/319. For data grids and tables that ask for the rows they show, and read from the header which ones they got and how many there are:

from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.ranges import PaginationRange, RangePage, RangeParams

ranges = PaginationRange(default_items=25, max_items=100)


@app.get("/contacts")
@cache(expire=60, tags=["contacts"])
async def contacts(params: Annotated[RangeParams, Depends(ranges)]) -> RangePage[Contact]:
    query = select(Contact).order_by(Contact.name).limit(params.limit).offset(params.offset)
    rows = (await session.scalars(query)).all()
    return ranges.paginate(rows, params, total=await count_contacts())
  • The range returned: end is the index of the last item in the response, which is short of the one asked for at the end of the list; null, and Content-Range: items */319, when there are none. limit is the size asked for, which the links keep.
  • From a database: query the range with params.offset and params.limit, and count: ranges.paginate(rows, params, total=count). Without total, paginate slices the range from the whole list.
  • Errors: without end, a range holds default_items. One whose end is before its start, or that holds more than max_items items, is a 400 before the endpoint runs; one that starts past the last item of a list that isn't empty, a 416 with Content-Range: items */<total>.
  • Links: first, previous, next and last ranges of the same size, the first and last on the grid of that size from 0. Pages served from the cache get their Content-Range too.
  • Its cost: like page numbers, a count on every range, and pages that shift when rows are added or deleted before them.

docs.title: PaginationScroll
docs.text:
A snapshot kept in the backend, read in batches: ?scroll_id=....

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

A scroll runs the query once and keeps what it found as a snapshot in the cache's backend, which the client reads in batches: what was there when the scroll started, whatever is written meanwhile. For exports, reports and jobs that read a whole result set while it changes, and for queries too costly to run once per page:

from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.scroll import PaginationScroll, ScrollPage, ScrollParams

scroll = PaginationScroll(Order, secret=settings.scroll_secret)  # secrets.token_urlsafe(32)


@app.get("/orders/export")
async def export(params: Annotated[ScrollParams, Depends(scroll)]) -> ScrollPage[Order]:
    if params.scroll_id is None:  # a new scroll: query once, one row more than it keeps
        query = select(Order).where(Order.status == "paid").order_by(Order.id)
        rows = await session.scalars(query.limit(scroll.max_items + 1))
        return await scroll.start(rows.all(), params)
    return await scroll.next(params)


@app.delete("/orders/export", status_code=204)
async def stop(scroll_id: str) -> None:
    await scroll.clear(scroll_id)

GET /orders/export?batch_size=100 answers the first batch, {"items": [...], "scroll_id": "WyJsR3Nq...", "total": 2450}, and ?scroll_id=<scroll_id> the next one; scroll_id is null after the last. The Link header has the next batch.

  • A snapshot: start writes the items into one entry of the backend, as JSON through their type (PaginationScroll(Order, ...)), and next reads them back as such. Rows added, changed or deleted meanwhile don't show, and no item is skipped or seen twice.
  • Kept alive while it's read: the snapshot lasts keep_alive seconds (60 by default) after each batch; a scroll_id whose snapshot has expired is a 404, and the client starts again. clear deletes it as soon as the client is done. The cache's own clear() leaves snapshots alone, and with a TieredBackend they're in the shared tier only.
  • Retries are safe: a scroll_id holds the snapshot's id and where the next batch starts, signed with HMAC-SHA256: the same request gets the same batch, and one made up or changed is a 400 before the endpoint runs. Each request may ask for its own batch_size, up to max_batch_size (1000 by default; a 422 beyond).
  • Who may read it: a scroll_id reads the rest of the snapshot without the endpoint's query running again, so whoever has one gets the results it was given for. When they depend on who asks, pass owner=str(user.id) to start, next and clear: a scroll_id is then only good for that user.
  • Sealed: the snapshot is sealed with the cache's signing_key, or encryption_key when it holds personal data, and one that someone planted in the backend is ignored.
  • Its limits: each batch reads the whole snapshot from the backend and writes it back to keep it alive, and each start keeps a new one, so start refuses more than max_items items (10,000 by default; query one more than that and it raises ValueError) and a rate limit on the endpoint keeps clients from starting scrolls without end. The snapshot is one entry: mind the backend's limit on the size of an entry (1 MB in Memcached, 400 KB in DynamoDB). A backend that fails is a 503, and the client retries. Don't put @cache on a scroll: each start must keep a snapshot of its own. To read a big table without keeping it anywhere, PaginationStreaming sends every row as it comes.

docs.title: PaginationSearchAfter
docs.text:
The sort values of the last item: ?search_after=["...",42]&limit=20.

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

The page after the sort values of the last item seen, given as a JSON array: ?search_after=["2026-10-29T10:00:00Z",42]. The values are plain, neither encoded nor signed: clients read them, and may write their own to start anywhere (the events since a date). Like a cursor, each page is a query through an index, and rows added or deleted meanwhile don't shift the pages. For exports, logs and searches that clients drive themselves:

from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.search_after import (
    PaginationSearchAfter,
    SearchAfterPage,
    SearchAfterParams,
)

events_after = PaginationSearchAfter(sort=(datetime, int))


@app.get("/events")
@cache(expire=60)
async def events(
    params: Annotated[SearchAfterParams, Depends(events_after)],
) -> SearchAfterPage[Event]:
    query = select(Event).order_by(Event.at, Event.id).limit(params.fetch)
    if params.search_after is not None:  # (at, id) of the last event seen
        query = query.where(tuple_(Event.at, Event.id) > params.search_after)
    rows = (await session.scalars(query)).all()
    return events_after.paginate(rows, params, key=lambda e: (e.at, e.id), queried=True)

GET /events?limit=20 answers {"items": [...], "limit": 20, "search_after": ["2026-10-29T09:58:30Z", 3]}, and ?search_after=["2026-10-29T09:58:30Z",3] (percent-encoded in the URL) the next page; search_after is null on the last one. The Link header has the first page and, except on the last, the next one.

  • Declared types: sort gives the types of the values, in order: int, float, str, bool, datetime (with a time zone), date, UUID and Decimal. params.search_after has them converted, and the page gives them as the items show them: datetimes and dates in ISO 8601, UUIDs and decimals as strings. A value of another type, another number of them or JSON that doesn't parse is a 400, and more than 1024 characters a 422, before the endpoint runs.
  • The key must be unique together: (e.at, e.id), not the time alone. key returns a tuple of the types of sort, and a value that isn't one is a TypeError.
  • Queried or sliced: with queried=True, the rows are those of the page, queried past params.search_after up to params.fetch (the limit and one more: it tells whether there's a next page). Without it, paginate finds the page in the whole sorted list. descending=True for newest first.
  • Readable and writable: nothing stops a client from asking for any position, so sort by what they may see. For a position they can't change, PaginationCursor seals the same key.
  • Forward only: to go back, clients keep the values they've used.

docs.title: PaginationStreaming
docs.text:
Every item as it comes, as NDJSON, without pages.

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

Every item in one response, as they come, without pages: NDJSON (application/x-ndjson), one JSON value per line, which a client reads while the rest is still being queried. For exports, for syncing everything to another system, and for scripts that would otherwise walk hundreds of pages. It isn't a dependency: it makes the response.

from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.streaming import PaginationStreaming

stream = PaginationStreaming(batch_size=100)


@app.get("/events")
async def events() -> StreamingResponse:
    async def fetch(after: int | None, limit: int) -> list[Event]:
        query = select(Event).order_by(Event.id).limit(limit)
        if after is not None:
            query = query.where(Event.id > after)
        return list((await session.scalars(query)).all())

    return stream.response(stream.batches(fetch, key=lambda e: e.id))

GET /events answers one event per line, {"id":1,...}, {"id":2,...}..., each hundred sent as soon as it's read, before the next hundred are queried, until the last event.

  • response(items) takes a list, a generator or an async iterable, and sends it in chunks of batch_size lines, models serialised with pydantic as FastAPI would. A synchronous generator is read in the thread pool, batch_size items at a time, so a blocking driver doesn't stop the event loop.
  • batches(fetch, key=...) reads a big table without loading it: fetch(None, batch_size), then fetch(key(last row), batch_size), until a batch comes back shorter than batch_size. Each query finds its batch through an index, as fast as the first. fetch can be sync or async, and key must be unique ((e.created_at, e.id) rather than e.created_at). It yields the rows one by one, ready for response().
  • max_items ends the response there, whatever is left (None, the default, for no end). The source is closed then, or at its end: a generator's finally runs.
  • A client that disconnects stops the stream: nothing more is read from the source, and no more queries are made.
  • Not cached: @cache doesn't keep streams, so each request reads the database again; don't put it on these endpoints.
  • Its limits: the status and headers go out before the first item, so an error halfway through can only cut the stream short; clients should check that they got what they expected (a count in another endpoint, or the last id). There's no resuming in the middle: a client that needs it pages by cursor instead.

docs.title: PaginationTimeBased
docs.text:
Before or after a time: ?timestamp=2026-10-29T10:00:00Z&limit=20.

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

Pages by time: ?timestamp=2026-10-29T10:00:00Z&limit=20 gives the items older than the timestamp, newest first (direction="older", for feeds), or newer than it, oldest first ("newer", for syncing). The timestamp is plain ISO 8601, which clients can read and write, and each page is a query through an index on the time:

from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.time_based import (
    PaginationTimeBased,
    TimeBasedPage,
    TimeBasedParams,
)

feed = PaginationTimeBased("older")


@app.get("/posts")
@cache(expire=60, tags=["posts"])
async def posts(params: Annotated[TimeBasedParams, Depends(feed)]) -> TimeBasedPage[Post]:
    query = select(Post).order_by(Post.posted_at.desc()).limit(params.fetch)
    if params.timestamp is not None:
        query = query.where(Post.posted_at < params.timestamp)
    rows = (await session.scalars(query)).all()
    return feed.paginate(rows, params, time=lambda p: p.posted_at, queried=True)

GET /posts?limit=20 answers {"items": [...], "limit": 20, "next_timestamp": "2026-10-29T10:00:00Z"}, the time of the page's last item, and ?timestamp=<next_timestamp> the next page; next_timestamp is null on the last one. The Link header has the first page and, except on the last, the next one.

  • Ties: the next page starts strictly past the last time, so a page never splits the items that share a time, or the next one would skip some. With queried=True, when the extra row of params.fetch (the limit and one) shares its time with the page's last items, they're left to the next page, which can make this one shorter; if that leaves nothing, more than limit items share one time, and paginate raises ValueError. Without it, paginate takes the rest of them from the whole list, past limit if need be.
  • Time zones: a timestamp without one is a 422, and the parameters hold it in UTC, so the same instant from another zone is the same cache entry. time must give datetimes with one too.
  • Syncing: with "newer", a client keeps the time of the last item it got (at the end, next_timestamp is null) and asks for the ones after it later.
  • Limits: when many items can share a time (imports, timestamps to the second), or rows can be written with a time already passed, paginate by a unique key with PaginationKeyset (the time and the id) instead.

docs.title: PaginationToken
docs.text:
An opaque token, bound to the query, that expires: ?page_token=...&page_size=20.

In an app: the example. How strategies work: Pagination. Every argument: the API reference.

A page token is the way to the next page and nothing else: opaque, signed, bound to the query it was issued for, and short-lived. Clients send back what the last page gave them and never build a page parameter of their own. For public APIs whose pagination may change behind the token without breaking anybody, and for lists whose filters must not be swapped halfway through:

from fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.page_token import PaginationToken, TokenPage, TokenParams

tokens = PaginationToken(settings.page_token_secret, ttl=600)  # secrets.token_urlsafe(32)


@app.get("/books")
@cache(expire=60)
async def books(
    params: Annotated[TokenParams, Depends(tokens)],
    genre: Genre | None = None,
) -> TokenPage[Book]:
    query = select(Book).order_by(Book.id).offset(params.offset).limit(params.fetch)
    if genre is not None:
        query = query.where(Book.genre == genre)
    rows = (await session.scalars(query)).all()
    return tokens.paginate(rows, params, queried=True)

GET /books?genre=poetry&page_size=20 answers {"items": [...], "next_page_token": "WzIwLC..."}, and ?genre=poetry&page_size=20&page_token=<next_page_token> the next page; next_page_token is null on the last one. The Link header has the next page.

  • What a token holds: the offset of the next page, a digest of the request's other query parameters (all but page_token and page_size, in any order) and when it was issued, signed with HMAC-SHA256 (secret is required; a list rotates secrets). A token that a client made or changed, that comes with other query parameters than its own, or that is older than ttl (3600 seconds by default) is a 400 before the endpoint runs. It's base64, not encrypted: clients can read the offset.
  • From a database: with queried=True, the rows are those of LIMIT params.fetch OFFSET params.offset, where fetch is page_size plus one: the extra row tells whether there's a next page. Without it, paginate slices the page from the whole list.
  • Limits: default_page_size=50, max_page_size=100; beyond the maximum, or a malformed token, is a 422. page_size may change from one page to the next.
  • Cached apart: the query's digest is part of TokenParams, so @cache keeps the pages of each query apart, even for parameters the endpoint doesn't read. A page served from the cache hands out the token issued when it was stored: keep expire well under ttl.
  • Its limits: forward only, with no total and no way to jump to a page. Underneath it's an offset, so rows added or deleted meanwhile shift the pages, and deep pages cost what OFFSET costs; for big lists that change, sort by key with PaginationCursor.

docs.title: Learn
docs.text:
Here is how to learn Alcazaba: a tutorial that starts with a quick start and takes each tool in turn, how to set it up for production, and complete example apps. Read the tutorial in order the first time; come back to a tool's page when you need it.

  • Tutorial - User Guide

    A first app in three steps, a cache, a rate limit and authorization, then a page per tool.

  • Production setup

    The configuration from the environment, and the state in Redis, shared by every process.

  • Examples

    Small, complete apps, each with a tool at work as it's meant to be used in production.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Here's the reference, or code API: every public class and function, by tool, with its parameters and what it raises. The Tutorial - User Guide tells how to use them, and the examples show them in complete apps.

  • Response cache

    Cache, FastAPICache, the @cache decorator, key builders and coders. In fastapi_alcazaba.response_cache.

  • Backends

    Where entries and state live: in memory, Redis, Valkey, GLIDE, memcached, DynamoDB, two levels. In fastapi_alcazaba.backends.

  • Pagination

    The twelve strategies, with their parameters and pages. In fastapi_alcazaba.pagination.

  • Rate and concurrency limits

    Requests per window and requests at a time, per client or shared, across processes. In fastapi_alcazaba.rate_limit.

  • Idempotency keys

    The middleware that replays the first response to a retried request. In fastapi_alcazaba.idempotency.

  • Authentication strategies

    FastAPIAuth, Strategy, and the JWT, bearer, OAuth2, SAML and session strategies. In fastapi_alcazaba.auth.

  • API keys, tokens and codes

    API keys stored as digests, revoked tokens and one-time codes. In fastapi_alcazaba.auth.

  • Authorization with Casbin

    A Casbin policy per route or for every request: FastAPICasbin and CasbinMiddleware. In fastapi_alcazaba.authz.

  • Sessions, CSRF and security headers

    What a cookie-based app needs: server-side sessions, CSRF protection, headers and body limits. In fastapi_alcazaba.security.

  • Audit trail

    FastAPIAudit, its entries and events, sinks, and the trail's verification. In fastapi_alcazaba.audit.

  • Checking uploads

    The type of a file from its bytes, its size and pixels, and safe file names. In fastapi_alcazaba.uploads.

  • Webhooks and outbound calls

    Standard Webhooks in and out, and httpx transports with deadlines, breakers and SSRF checks. In fastapi_alcazaba.webhooks and fastapi_alcazaba.outbound.

  • Errors and observability

    Problem details, request IDs, request deadlines and health checks. In fastapi_alcazaba.observability.

  • Background work

    Scheduled jobs, the task queue, leader election and locks shared by every process. In fastapi_alcazaba.background.

  • Operations

    Circuit breakers, maintenance mode and feature flags, switched at runtime. In fastapi_alcazaba.operations.

  • Integrity, resilience and errors

    What signs and encrypts entries, RFC 8785 canonical JSON, the backends' circuit breaker, and the exceptions. In fastapi_alcazaba.core.

FastAPIAudit, its entries and events, sinks, and the trail's verification. In fastapi_alcazaba.audit.

In the guide: Audit trail. In an app: the example.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.audit.FastAPIAudit
docs.text:
FastAPIAudit(sinks: Iterable[AuditSink] | None = None, *, signing_key: Secrets | None = None, redact: Collection[str] = (), timeout: float = 5.0, metrics: Metrics | None = None)

An audit trail: action() records what endpoints do, record() and log() the rest.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default sinks Iterable[AuditSink] | None

where the events go; a LoggingAuditSink by default.

None signing_key Secrets | None

signs and chains the events (see verify_audit_trail); a secret of at least 32 bytes, or several to rotate it (the first signs). The same in every process.

None redact Collection[str]

words that mark secrets in the keys of details, besides SENSITIVE_WORDS.

() timeout float

seconds each sink has to write an event.

5.0 metrics Metrics | None

where to count the events (fastapi_alcazaba.audit) and those not written (fastapi_alcazaba.audit.undelivered); FastAPICache's by default.

None

docs.title: action
docs.text:
action(name: str, *, resource: str | None = None) -> Callable[[HTTPConnection], AsyncIterator[AuditEntry]]

A dependency that records the action name when the endpoint ends, and gives the endpoint its AuditEntry to fill in (actor, details...). resource is a template of the path parameters, such as "invoice:{invoice_id}", filled in before anything runs: the requests refused are recorded with it too.

docs.title: record async
docs.text:
record(action: str, *, actor: str | int | UUID | None = None, resource: str | int | UUID | None = None, details: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, request: HTTPConnection | None = None) -> AsyncIterator[AuditEntry]

Records the block as the action action, when it ends: outside endpoints (jobs, tasks, commands), or around a part of one. request adds the request's method, route and client.

docs.title: log async
docs.text:
log(action: str, *, outcome: Outcome = 'success', actor: str | int | UUID | None = None, resource: str | int | UUID | None = None, reason: str | None = None, details: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, request: HTTPConnection | None = None) -> AuditEvent

Writes one event and returns it, e.g. for a failed login. request adds the request's method, route and client.

docs.title: fastapi_alcazaba.audit.AuditEntry
docs.text:
AuditEntry(action: str, *, actor: str | int | UUID | None = None, resource: str | int | UUID | None = None, details: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None)

The event an action writes when it ends: the endpoint fills in what it learns.

outcome is decided by how the action ends; set it ("denied", "failure") when the endpoint returns an error response instead of raising one. reason says why it failed or was denied, the exception's type by default.

docs.text:
actor: str | None

Who does it, e.g. the user's ID.

What it's done to, e.g. "invoice:42".

docs.text:
AuditEvent(id: str, time: datetime, action: str, outcome: Outcome, actor: str | None = None, resource: str | None = None, reason: str | None = None, status: int | None = None, request_id: str | None = None, trace_id: str | None = None, method: str | None = None, route: str | None = None, client: str | None = None, details: Mapping[str, Any] = dict(), stream: str = '', sequence: int = 0, previous: str | None = None, signature: str | None = None)

An event of the trail, as the sinks get it; to_dict() and to_json() give its JSON form.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default id str

random, unique.

required time datetime

when it was written (UTC).

required action str

what was done, e.g. "invoice.delete".

required outcome Outcome

success, failure or denied.

required actor str | None

who did it (a user's ID), if known.

None resource str | None

what it was done to, e.g. "invoice:42".

None reason str | None

why it failed or was denied: the exception's type, or the reason given.

None status int | None

the HTTP status of the exception that ended it.

None request_id str | None

the request's ID (RequestIDMiddleware).

None trace_id str | None

the OpenTelemetry trace it belongs to.

None method str | None

the request's HTTP method.

None route str | None

the template of the route that matched, e.g. "/invoices/{invoice_id}".

None client str | None

the client's address, as the server reports it.

None details Mapping[str, Any]

anything else, redacted and bounded.

dict() stream str

the writer's stream: one per process and FastAPIAudit.

'' sequence int

its number in the stream, from 1.

0 previous str | None

the signature of the stream's previous event (with a signing_key).

None signature str | None

with a signing_key, HMAC-SHA256 in hex of fastapi_alcazaba/audit2, a NUL byte, and the RFC 8785 canonical JSON of to_dict() without signature: a verifier in any language computes the same.

None
